short_description: Myelography, posterior fossa, radiological supervision and interpretation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs imaging supervision and interpretation of a procedure to image the posterior cranial fossa using a contrast medium. He performs the procedure to diagnose a possible brain tumor. A patient with a brain tumor of the posterior cranial fossa may have balance problems and difficulty walking straight. Explanation This code represents the technical and professional components of a service. The provider performs radiographic diagnostic study of the posterior cranial fossa while utilizing fluoroscopy imaging for the assessment of any intracranial pathology. He performs a lumbar puncture and injects contrast material into the subarachnoid space to enhance image sequences. He supervises the performance of the entire radiological procedure and interprets the findings. The provider who performs imaging supervision and interpretation for this procedure reports this code. Terminology Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Lumbar puncture: The provider inserts a needle into the lumbar (lower back) area; for the diagnostic lumbar puncture, the provider collects cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to test for infections or hemorrhages; for the therapeutic lumbar puncture, the provider injects medication into the CSF to provide anesthesia or to administer chemotherapy; also known as a spinal tap. Microsurgical techniques: Procedures employing very small instruments while viewing the surgical field through an operative microscope. Myelography: Radiography of the spinal canal by injecting contrast agent through a needle into the space around the spinal cord. Posterior cranial fossa: A small space in the skull, found near the brainstem, responsible for controlling vital body functions, such as breathing, and the cerebellum, the part of the brain responsible for movement, balance, and coordination. Radiographic: Pertaining to X–rays and, by extension, other imaging procedures. Subarachnoid space: The space between the innermost and the middle of the three meninges, or membranes, that protect the spinal cord and brain. Tips There may be rare instances where one provider supervises the radiology service and another provider interprets it. According to Medicare guidelines, each provider should report the radiology code and append reduced service modifier 52. Each should also append modifier 26 to the code to report only the professional component. To assign a code whose descriptor includes contrast, the contrast must be intravascular, intraarticular, or intrathecal. Depending on the payer’s guidelines, providers who supply contrast may also separately report the contrast using a 99070 supply code or a HCPCS Level II code. Check individual payers’ policies for contrast coverage and reportable supply codes. If you are reporting only the interpretation or professional component for X–rays taken using portable equipment, you should report the same service code from the 70010 to 79999, Radiology procedures, range that you would report for nonportable services. Report a place of service, or POS, code reflecting where the doctor performed his service. Read Less

short_description: Magnetic resonance (eg, proton) imaging, temporomandibular joint(s)
lay_term: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a noninvasive medical test that helps physicians diagnose and treat medical conditions .MR imaging uses a magnetic field, radio frequency pulses and uses the natural magnetic properties of the hydrogen atoms in our body that emit radiofrequency signals when exposed to radio waves in an electro–magnetic field. A computer produces detailed 3D tomographic pictures of soft tissues and all other internal body structures. MRI does not use ionizing radiation (X–rays).Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the primary modality for the evaluation of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). MRI provides sharp tissue contrast for visualizing the soft tissue and periarticular structures of the TMJ and study intra–articular abnormalities with the use of dedicated coils and high spatial resolution. Dynamic maneuvers (opening and closing the mouth) are necessary part of the examination. Explanation The physician places the patient on a sliding table and a radio antenna device called a surface coil is positioned around the upper part of the head. After positioning the patient with the head inside the MRI gantry, the physician/technologist leaves the room and the individual MRI sequences are performed. Depending on how many images are needed, the exam will generally take 15 to 45 minutes, although a very detailed study takes longer. The patient is asked not to move during the actual imaging process, but between sequences some movement is allowed. Patient is required to remain still for only a few seconds at a time. Some patients are given an injection of a contrast material to enhance the visibility of certain tissues or blood vessels. A small needle connected to an intravenous line is placed in an arm or hand vein. A saline solution drips through the intravenous line to prevent clotting until the contrast material is injected about two–thirds of the way through the exam. When the exam is over the patient is asked to wait until the images are examined to determine if more images are needed. Report this code if MRI of temporomandibular joint(s) (TMJ) is performed. Terminology Temporomandibular joint (TMJ): A type of ball and socket joint that forms the union of the temporal bone at the base of the cranium (skull) and the mandible (lower jaw bone) and facilitates movement of the lower jaw. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI): A technique of visualizing soft tissues of the body's interior by applying an external magnetic field. Read Less

short_description: Computed tomography, orbit, sella, or posterior fossa or outer, middle, or inner ear; with contrast material(s)
lay_term: The provider uses computed tomography, or CT, to examine the eye’s orbit, the sella or posterior fossa of the skull, or the outer, middle, or inner ear. The provider administers contrast for this exam. Explanation The provider performs an injection of contrast material. The provider positions the patient on the table that slides into the CT scanner. The patient remains still while the provider uses the scanner to take X–ray images of the target anatomy of the orbit, sella, posterior fossa, or ear structures. From these scans, a computer creates images called slices. The images help the provider identify tumors and other anatomic abnormalities as well as foreign bodies. Terminology Computed tomography: Computed tomography, or CT, is when the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Intrathecal: In the area under the protective membrane, called the arachnoid membrane, covering the spinal cord or brain. Orbit: Bony cavity that holds the eyes; the orbital area is formed by seven bones, the frontal, lacrimal, ethmoid, zygomatic, maxillary, palatine, and sphenoid bones. Posterior fossa: A small space near the base of the skull; near the brainstem and cerebellum, part of the hindbrain important for movement. Sella: A saddle shaped depression at the skull’s base that holds the small, hormone producing pituitary gland; the sella is also called the sella turcica. Tips For a similar study without contrast, see 70480, Computed tomography, orbit, sella, or posterior fossa or outer, middle, or inner ear; without contrast materials. When the provider administers oral or rectal contrast, you should code the service as without contrast because the radiology service includes oral and rectal contrast. To assign a code whose descriptor includes contrast, the contrast must be intravascular, intraarticular, or intrathecal. Depending on the payer’s guidelines, providers who supply contrast may also separately report the contrast using a 99070 supply code or a HCPCS Level II code. Check individual payers’ policies for contrast coverage and reportable supply codes. If you are reporting only the physician’s interpretation for the radiology service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the radiology code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the radiology service, you would append modifier TC to the radiology code. Note, however, that payer policy may exempt hospitals from appending modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the radiology code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Read Less

short_description: Radiologic examination, spine, lumbosacral; 2 or 3 views
lay_term: The technician takes 2 or 3 views of the vertebrae in the lumbar region which is the lower part of the spine and the sacrum, the area that connects the spine to the pelvis. Lumbosacral spine X–rays help evaluate back injuries, persistent numbness, and low back pain. Explanation The patient lies on the X–ray table in different positions while the technician takes two or three views of the lower part of the spine and the sacrum, the area that connects the spine to the pelvis. When the X–ray is being done to diagnose an injury, care is taken to prevent further injury. The X–ray machine is placed over the lower part of the patient's spine. The patient is asked to hold his breath as the picture is taken so that the image is not blurred. During the examination, an X–ray machine sends a beam of radiation through the back, and an image is recorded on a computer or special film. Dense body parts such as bones appear white on the X–ray image as they absorb much of radiation. Two or three images are taken during this procedure. Terminology Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine and protect the spinal cord; there are 33 segments divided into five different levels — the neck (cervical spine, C1 through C7), upper and middle back (thoracic spine, T1 through T12), lower back (lumbar, L1 through L5), sacral (sacrum, S1 through S5), and tail bone (coccyx which consists of 4 fused bones). Tips This exam includes two or three views of the lumbar spine which may include the AP (anteroposterior) view, which means the tech takes this view from front to back through the body; a lateral view, which is taken from the patient's side; or a cone–down view, an additional lateral view of the spine focused more on a specific part than the normal lateral view. In a typical lateral image, the pelvis bones are superimposed over the spine. Cone–down views result in clearer pictures and allow the radiologist to better visualize the lower lumbosacral spine and the joint space. You may see this view called the "L5/S1 spot." When the provider performs a minimum of four views of the lumbosacral spine, use code 72110. When the provider performs a complete, or minimum of six views, of the lumbosacral spine, use code 72114. short_description: Magnetic resonance angiography, spinal canal and contents, with or without contrast material(s)
lay_term: In this diagnostic procedure, the provider performs magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of blood vessels of the spinal canal and contents to check for stenosis or an aneurysm of the vessels. The provider may use contrast during the procedure. Explanation Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) is an MRI examination of the blood vessels. The provider uses this procedure to generate images of arteries and veins to evaluate them for stenosis or aneurysm. The scanning table slides the patient’s whole body into a large tunnel shaped magnetic scanner so that patient's spinal canal is inside a strong magnetic field. Contrast material may be injected into the patient’s blood vessels to enhance the images. The provider captures the radiofrequency signals generated by the body and the computer generates a series of images that displays the vascular structure of the spinal canal. Next, the provider reviews the images, does his analysis, and interprets the results. Finally, the provider prepares a written report of his findings. Terminology Aneurysm: Weakness in the wall of a blood vessel or wall of a ventricle of the heart, typically the left ventricle, causing the wall to balloon out; sometimes requiring surgical excision or repair to prevent rupture. Arteries: Vessels that carry oxygen rich blood away from the heart to the rest of the body. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Stenosis: Narrowing of a vessel or other structure. Vein: Vessels that carry oxygen poor blood from the body to the heart. Tips If you are reporting only the physician’s interpretation for the radiology service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the radiology code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the radiology service, you would append modifier TC to the radiology code. Note, however, that payer policy may exempt hospitals from appending modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the radiology code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. When the provider administers oral or rectal contrast, you should code the service as without contrast because the radiology service includes oral and rectal contrast. To assign a code whose descriptor includes contrast, the contrast must be intravascular, intraarticular, or intrathecal. Depending on the payer’s guidelines, providers who supply contrast may also separately report the contrast using a 99070 supply code or a HCPCS Level II code. Check individual payers’ policies for contrast coverage and reportable supply codes. Read Less

short_description: Radiologic examination, sacroiliac joints; less than 3 views
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider takes one or two X–ray views of the sacroiliac joints to check for any fracture, swelling, or reason of pain in the lower back area. Explanation An X–ray of the sacroiliac joints uses a small amount of radiation to take images of the joint between the sacrum and the ilium. The X–ray machine sends a beam of radiation through the joint. Dense body parts that block the passage of the X–ray beam through the body, such as bones, appear white on the X–ray image. Softer body tissues, such as muscles and fat, allow the X–ray beams to pass through them and appear darker. short_description: Magnetic resonance (eg, proton) imaging, abdomen; without contrast material(s), followed by with contrast material(s) and further sequences
lay_term: The provider performs magnetic resonance imaging of the structures and organs of the abdomen, initially without control and then with additional sequences after injection of contrast. Explanation Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a noninvasive diagnostic imaging study that helps physicians diagnose and treat medical conditions. MRI uses a magnetic field, radio frequency pulses and uses the natural magnetic properties of the hydrogen atoms in our body that emit radiofrequency signals when exposed to radio waves in an electro–magnetic field. A computer produces detailed 3D tomographic pictures of organs, soft tissues and all other internal body structures. MRI does not use ionizing radiation (X–rays). It also can find tissue damage or disease, such as infection or a tumor. This study is initially performed without administration of intravenous contrast material and then repeated while injecting intravascular contrast through patient's vein. A radiologic agent or a dye may be used as contrast material which is injected through a small catheter placed in the vein of the arm or hand. The patient is asked not to eat or drink for a few hours before the test. The technician who operates the machine will be in another room and always able to watch or hear the patient during the exam. The patient is placed supine on the MRI table which slides the whole body into a large tunnel–shaped magnetic scanner so that patient's abdomen is inside a strong magnetic field. The technician instructs the patient to hold his breath and stay still for 10–15 seconds while the images are taken. During the test, the MRI makes a rapid tapping noise. To mask this noise earplugs are provided to the patient. Images are obtained prior to the administration of contrast material. Contrast material is then administered, and additional images are obtained. A technician will capture the radiofrequency signals generated by the body and a computer will generate a series of images that display slices of the target area. Pictures from an MRI scan are digital images that are displayed on the computer screen. The physician reviews both the non–contrast and contrast images and forms a diagnostic impression which is written into a report. Terminology Contrast material: Material taken orally or injected intravenously that helps to produce more clear and distinct image of the particular organ under the study. Tips For MRI abdomen without contrast, see 74181. For MRI abdomen with contrast, see 74182. Explanation For a diagnostic exam commonly called a barium swallow or esophagram, the provider positions the patient on an X–ray table. The provider evaluates the function and appearance of the esophagus as well as the swallowing process. The provider may reposition the patient during the exam. short_description: Computed tomographic (CT) colonography, screening, including image postprocessing Notes: (Do not report 74263 in conjunction with 72192-72194, 74150-74170, 74261, 74262, 76376, 76377)
lay_term: In this exam, the provider performs a noninvasive imaging method called computed tomography (CT) to examine the colon and produce high–resolution two– and three–dimensional images for colorectal polyps and cancer screening. CT colonography (CTC) is also known as virtual colonoscopy or virtual colonography. Explanation After the patient completes a thorough colon cleansing like that used for a colonoscopy and is properly prepped, the provider positions the patient on a movable table and inserts a soft–tipped catheter into the rectum. He then pumps room air or carbon dioxide into the colon to distend the colon for better viewing. He slides the table into the center of a large donut–shaped machine or CT scanner. The provider passes thin beam X–rays from the scanner. X–ray detectors in the equipment pick them up and feed the information into the computer that produces images on a monitor in different colors or in gray scale. The images are a slice, or cross–section, of a thin segment of the body. The color variations reflect tissue density based on the amount of radiation that passes through. The provider places the patient in different positions to help ensure the sufficient distention of all the segments of the colon, to shift any remaining fluid within the colon so it doesn’t hide polyps, and to help differentiate stool, which will move around, from polyps that are stationary. Computed tomography (CT): A noninvasive imaging technique, where the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer–generated cross–sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. When he injects the radiopaque contrast material in the patient's arm in the vein, it flows through the patient’s blood stream and resides in the kidneys and urinary tract and enables him to take an X–ray. This code represents both the technical and professional components of the service. short_description: Magnetic resonance (eg, proton) imaging, fetal, including placental and maternal pelvic imaging when performed; single or first gestation
lay_term: Fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses magnetic fields and radio waves, which are converted by a computer to three–dimensional images, to examine the unborn baby from different angles and identify any abnormality in developing fetus. The procedure may include imaging of the placenta and the maternal pelvis. Fetal MRI helps to examine the structure of organs or other tissues of the unborn baby and identify any abnormality related to the child’s development during gestation. This code applies to the first gestation or a single fetus. Explanation During the diagnostic procedure, the provider places the patient on a scanning table that slides the whole body into a large tunnel–shaped magnetic scanner, which passes a magnetic field through the patient and fetus. short_description: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging for morphology and function without contrast material(s), followed by contrast material(s) and further sequences
lay_term: The provider uses cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to examine the structure and function of heart. She initiates the procedure without administration of contrast and follows it with administration of contrast. Explanation Cardiac MRI is a radiological imaging technique that provides three–dimensional images of any defects or abnormality present in the heart. The provider removes any foreign object or metal from the patient’s body and makes the patient lie in a narrow tunnel that has an MRI machine at the other end. She takes several images of the cross section of heart. The characteristic magnetic properties of MRI use hydrogen from the patient’s body and transmit signals that create strong electromagnetic fields. This electromagnetic field produces high resolution images. The provider initially obtains images without administration of contrast and then administers contrast to obtain images. She repeats this sequence of contrast for each slide. Terminology Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Electromagnetic field: A physical field that has combination with both electric charges in motion; consists of two components, electric and magnetic components and is responsible for changing the nature of objects. Heart rate: Number of heart beats per unit time. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI): An imaging technique to visualize soft tissues of the body's interior by applying an external magnetic field and radio waves to create 3–dimensional images of body parts. Morphology: Study of the shape and structure. Stress imaging: The provider monitors the heart rate while the patient performs strenuous activity like exercising on treadmill. Velocity flow mapping: The study measures the flow of blood volume in the ascending and descending aorta. Tips If the provider examines the structure and function of the heart without administrating any contrast agent, use 75557, Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging for morphology and function without contrast material. If the provider performs cardiac MRI to study the structure and function of heart without contrast, along with stress imaging, use 75559, Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging for morphology and function without contrast material; with stress imaging. If the provider performs cardiac MRI to study the structure and function of heart without contrast and then with contrast along with stress imaging, use 75563, Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging for morphology and function without contrast material(s), followed by contrast material(s) and further sequences; with stress imaging. Explanation Computed tomography (CT) uses an X–ray tube or detectors to produce cross sectional images to examine any defect or abnormality in the heart. The provider introduces contrast material at regular intervals in the vein of the arm and examines the heart via the X–ray beam. He makes the patient lie on a table that has a CT machine at the other end. short_description: Shuntogram for investigation of previously placed indwelling nonvascular shunt (eg, LeVeen shunt, ventriculoperitoneal shunt, indwelling infusion pump), radiological supervision and interpretation Notes: (For procedure, see 49427 or 61070)
lay_term: The provider performs supervision and interpretation of radiologic imaging to examine a previously placed indwelling infusion pump or a nonvascular shunt, such as a shunt between a ventricle in the brain and the peritoneum or a shunt between the abdomen and superior vena cava. Explanation This code may represent either the technical component for a facility or the professional component for a provider. For this procedure, the provider inserts a needle and injects contrast material into a previously placed shunt, such as a ventriculoperitoneal or LeVeen shunt or an indwelling infusion pump reservoir. The provider then takes images to evaluate the flow of contrast to examine drainage through the shunt. The provider who performs imaging supervision and interpretation for this procedure reports this code. Terminology Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Le Veen shunt: A surgically placed tube that connects the peritoneal cavity with the superior vena cava to drain ascitic fluid from the peritoneal cavity which is the space between the parietal peritoneum, the membrane that lines the abdominal cavity, and the visceral peritoneum, the part of the peritoneum that covers the abdominal organs; the peritoneal cavity is normally free of fluid except for just enough to keep the membrane surfaces moist. Shunt: A surgically created anastomosis or an implanted tube which diverts the flow of blood or other fluid from one site to another. Shuntogram: Radiographic imaging to evaluate the functioning of a shunt. Ventriculoperitoneal shunt: A surgically placed tube between a ventricle of the brain and the peritoneum, the membrane lining the abdominal cavity, to drain excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from a ventricle in the brain. Indwelling infusion pump: A drug reservoir connected to a small pump that delivers a drug, such as a chemotherapy drug or pain medicine, at a programmed rate; the reservoir can be refilled using an external needle port. Tips If you are reporting only the provider interpretation for the radiology service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the radiology code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the radiology service, you would append modifier TC to the radiology code. Note, however, that payer policy may exempt hospitals from appending modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the radiology code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. You should report the injection procedure separately using code 49427, Injection procedure, e.g., contrast media, for evaluation of previously placed peritoneal venous shunt, or 61070, Puncture of shunt tubing or reservoir for aspiration or injection procedure. There may be rare instances where one provider supervises the radiology service and another provider interprets it. According to Medicare guidelines, each provider should report the radiology code and append reduced service modifier 52. Each should also append modifier 26 to the code to report only the professional component. In a previously placed shunt, the provider may order a shuntogram to test the effectiveness of the shunt. Radiology codes such as shuntography are often components of other codes. If an edit is allowed to be made with a modifier, you must provide documentation that the radiology service was separately identifiable, medically necessary, and diagnostic in nature. Read Less

short_description: Percutaneous transhepatic portography with hemodynamic evaluation, radiological supervision and interpretation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs imaging supervision and interpretation for percutaneous transhepatic portography. The provider injects contrast medium in the bile duct through a needle or catheter in the liver’s portal vein. He visualizes and checks the patency, or openness, of the portal system. The service includes hemodynamic evaluation, which provides a clear picture of blood pressure, blood flow, and how well the body transports oxygen in the blood to body tissues. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a needle or catheter into a transhepatic site in the bile duct or via the right portal vein. He then injects a contrast medium into the body at the site. The provider uses fluoroscopy to examine the movement of the contrast medium through the portal system. The provider performs a hemodynamic evaluation, checking items such as blood pressure, blood flow, and oxygen levels. He then removes the needle or catheter, checks for bleeding, and closes the site based on patient needs. The provider who performs imaging supervision and interpretation for this procedure reports this code. Terminology Bile ducts: Channels, or tubes, that carry bile from the liver to the gallbladder for storage and ultimately draining into the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine; the bile ducts, also known as the biliary tree, include the common bile duct, cystic duct, and hepatic ducts. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Fluoroscopy: A live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Portography:A technique for visualizing the hepatic portal system, which allows blood to move from the stomach, intestines, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder to the liver. Transhepatic: Directly through the bile duct; e.g., direct injection into a bile duct for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes. Tips An example of a code you may report for the catheterization involved in this procedure is 36481, Percutaneous portal vein catheterization by any method. If the provider performs a similar service without hemodynamic evaluation use 75587, Percutaneous transhepatic portography without hemodynamic evaluation, radiological supervision and interpretation. If you are reporting only the physician’s interpretation for the radiology service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the radiology code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the radiology service, you would append modifier TC to the radiology code. Note, however, that payer policy may exempt hospitals from appending modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the radiology code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. There may be rare instances where one provider supervises the radiology service and another provider interprets it. According to Medicare guidelines, each provider should report the radiology code and append reduced service modifier 52. Each should also append modifier 26 to the code to report only the professional component. Read Less

short_description: Endovascular repair of descending thoracic aorta (eg, aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, dissection, penetrating ulcer, intramural hematoma, or traumatic disruption); involving coverage of left subclavian artery origin, initial endoprosthesis plus descending thoracic aortic extension(s), if required, to level of celiac artery origin, radiological supervision and interpretation Notes: (For implantation of endovascular graft, use 33880)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs imaging supervision and interpretation for the repair of the descending thoracic aorta. He uses arteriography to visualize the inside of the blood vessels and to identify and repair an aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous malformation, or trauma to the descending thoracic aorta by using an endoprosthesis. The provider places the endoprosthesis at the target site in the descending thoracic aorta covering the origin of the left subclavian artery. He may also extend the prosthesis to the level of the celiac artery origin. An aneurysm is a bulge in the blood vessel due to a weak area in the wall of the vessel. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the skin of the groin or arm. In either approach he then, under separately reportable fluoroscopic guidance, uses a guide wire to introduce an endoprosthesis, which is usually a plastic tube, through the femoral or other artery and places it at the site of the aneurysm in the descending thoracic aorta covering the origin of the left subclavian artery. This plastic tube is a holding device that anchors the weakness in the wall of the artery. He then may further use a stent and balloon angioplasty in which he guides a balloon catheter, again using fluoroscopy, until it reaches the first component, and inflates the balloon to seat the component and to further reinforce the stability of the repair. He repeats the steps as necessary to deploy a second and subsequent components that overlap, without covering the celiac origin. He performs imaging and contrast injections as needed during the procedure to confirm anatomy and proper component placement. If necessary, he may also place an extension prosthesis to cover the origin of the celiac artery. Still using fluoroscopic guidance, he guides the extension component through the artery to the arch, and through the previously seated components to position and deploy the device. He may again advance a balloon catheter using fluoroscopy to seat the device and stop the leak. He confirms the repair, checks for leaks, and evaluates nearby vessels for tears, clots, or any narrowing of a vessel. Finally, when the procedure is complete, he removes the catheter and wires, and then closes the wound by suturing the skin incision. The provider who performs imaging supervision and interpretation for this procedure reports this code. Aorta: The main artery of the body, which arises from the heart and supplies oxygenated blood to the rest of the body; in humans it passes from the left ventricle of heart and runs down to the backbone. Arch of aorta: The second section of the aorta following the ascending aorta. Arteries: Vessels that carry oxygen rich blood away from the heart to the rest of the body. Arteriovenous malformation: Abnormal tangle formed between arteries and veins. Balloon angioplasty: A procedure in which the provider opens the narrowed artery by using a balloon to open the blockage. Balloon catheter: A flexible tube with a balloon at the tip that can be inflated and deflated with a mechanism at the other end. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Celiac artery: An artery that originates from the abdominal aorta and branches to supply the oxygenated blood to stomach, liver, and spleen. Endoprosthesis: An intravascular device like a hollow stent that is placed into a duct to allow drainage through a blockage area or to act as a replacement for damaged ductal or vessel walls. Endovascular: Through the blood vessel. Femoral artery: The main blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood to the legs. Fluoroscopy: A live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Guide wire: A flexible wire inserted through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and other items such as stents. Iliac artery: An artery that supplies blood to the lower half of the body including pelvis, buttock, and the groin. Intramural hematoma: Leakage of blood within the aortic wall. Prosthesis: An artificial or synthetic material or device a provider uses to replace a body part or tissues. Pseudoaneurysm: Also, known as false aneurysm, is dilation in the artery causing leakage of blood. Stent: A thin expandable tube placed through a narrowed area of a tubular structure, such as the esophagus, small intestine, or a vessel, to prevent obstruction and provide support after dilation. Subclavian artery: One of the arteries that comes off the aortic arch and feeds the upper body. Ulcer: An open sore on external or internal surface of the body, caused by a break in the skin which fails to heal; it can be a small, painful sore or serious lesion. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs imaging supervision and interpretation during placement of extension prosthesis at the site where he previously repairs abnormalities such as those listed in the descriptor including an aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm of the descending thoracic aorta. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the skin of the groin. Next, under separately reportable fluoroscopic guidance, he uses a guide wire to introduce the extension prosthesis, which is usually a stent and places it at the site of the aneurysm or other artery abnormality. He then expands the stent at the site of weakness in the vessel. Next, he may introduce a balloon catheter, and inflate the balloon at the stent site to fully expand the stent to anchor the blood vessel. Finally, when the procedure is complete he removes the catheter and closes the wound by suturing the skin incision. The provider who performs imaging supervision and interpretation for this procedure reports this code. Arteries: Vessels that carry oxygen rich blood away from the heart to the rest of the body. Balloon catheter: A flexible tube with a balloon at the tip that can be inflated and deflated with a mechanism at the other end. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. lay_term: Trained clinical staff assess magnetic resonance (MR) safety based on implants or foreign bodies the patient has. This code represents the first 15 minutes and includes a written report. Explanation Trained clinical staff assess magnetic resonance (MR) safety based on implants or foreign bodies in the patient’s body. These items can put the patient at risk of injury or death during MR services, including diagnostic imaging or MR imaging guidance. For this service, the assessment includes identifying and verifying the implant components using various sources such as surgical reports, imaging studies, medical device databases, and device vendors. guidelines: Radiology Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Implanted medical devices or foreign bodies can increase the risk of injury or death for a patient entering the magnetic resonance (MR) environment, either for diagnostic MR procedures or for procedures performed under MR imaging guidance. Implants may have FDA-approved labeling specifying conditions under which an MR examination could be safely performed. These conditions can specify the type of MR equipment to use, preparation of the implant before the MR procedure, anatomical regions that should be excluded from MR examination, limitations on MR scan time and energy deposition, and/or implant components that may contraindicate MR examination. Codes 76014, 76015, 76016 describe MR safety-planning services performed in advance of the date of the MR procedure. For 76014, implant-safety conditions and additional procedures required to safely perform the requested MR examination are documented for inclusion in the medical record by a technologist or other MR safety-trained clinical staff. Contraindications to MR are also documented. For patients with complex, multiple, or incompletely documented implants, use 76015 to report prolonged MR safety implant/foreign body assessment by clinical staff. For an implant and/or foreign body that lacks MR conditional labeling, is contraindicated for MR, or may result in a limited MR examination, use 76016 to report the performance of an MR safety determination by a physician or other qualified health care professional (QHP) responsible for the safe performance of the MR procedure, with a written report. Codes 76017, 76018, 76019 describe MR safety services performed on the day of the MR examination under supervision of the physician or other QHP responsible for the safe performance of the MR procedure. The need for these services depends on the design of the medical implant, and the MR conditional labeling of the implant, if available. Use 76017 to report medical physics services provided during the MR examination, with a written report. Use 76018 to report the preparation and documentation of an electronic implant into an MR-protective mode. Use 76019 to report specified positioning and/or immobilization of an implant during the MR examination, with documentation for inclusion in the medical record. Cardiac devices (eg, pacemakers and defibrillators) may require interrogation or programming services before or after the performance of the MR examination to put them in a mode safe for the MR scan. For cardiac device interrogation or programming, see the appropriate cardiac device evaluation code. Similarly, neurostimulation devices may require analysis-programming before being placed into an MR-protective mode, or after the performance of the MR examination. For electronic analysis-programming of neurostimulation devices, see the appropriate analysis-programming code. If cardiac device evaluation or neurostimulator analysis-programming is performed on the same day, report 76018 only if a separate individual performs additional preparation of the electronic implant into an MR-protective mode immediately before patient entry to the MR environment. For reprogramming of programmable cerebrospinal shunt after the performance of the MR examination, use 62252.

lay_term: The provider uses special X–ray equipment that allows viewing of only one plane of the body based upon complex movements of the equipment and scanning across the body in one direction. Images show one plane in focus, and the other sections above and below the plane are blurred. Explanation The provider uses special X–ray equipment that allows viewing of only one plane of the body. He images one slice in focus and blurs out all other sections above and below that particular level. This technique emphasizes the one plane of the body or structure and produces sharper images of the structure being studied with minimal superimposition of other structures. This type of X–ray is called tomography and is possible because the X–ray tube and film move simultaneously. The images the provider captures help evaluate and locate lesions accurately in places like the lungs and bones. Terminology Body plane: Specific sections or regions of the body created by imaginary lines that form a flat surface and divide the body. Tomography: X–ray technique that produces a slice of an object, showing one plane in focus while the sections above and below are blurred, which is possible as the X–ray tube and the film move synchronously. Urography: X–ray examination to check the kidneys and the ureters, or tubes, that drain the kidneys. This service visualizes biomechanics (movement) of the body such as vocal cord movement, heart cycle, or dynamic motion of the spine or joints. short_description: Computed tomography, limited or localized follow-up study
lay_term: In this exam, the provider performs a subsequent computed tomography restricted to a specific area to be imaged or treated. This type of noninvasive technique is used to reexamine the patient if an ordering provider suspects complications or a tumor. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and positioned on a movable table, the table slides into the center of a large donut–shaped machine, called a CT scanner. The provider then uses the machine to take multiple X–ray images of a specific location or suspect structure as the X–ray beam moves in a circle around the body. The rotation allows many pictures of the same area to be taken from many angles and then the computer puts them together to produce and display a 3D image on a monitor for interpretation. short_description: Magnetic resonance spectroscopy Notes: (For magnetic resonance imaging, use appropriate MRI body site code) (For magnetic resonance spectroscopy, determination and localization of discogenic pain, see 0609T, 0610T)
lay_term: The provider uses a diagnostic imaging technique called magnetic resonance spectroscopy or MRS to detect and identify the chemical composition of diseased tissue and structures or to study the metabolism of organs. MRS is similar to a conventional magnetic resonance imaging or MRI, and a provider may perform it as part of a routine MRI, but an MRI examines body structure where an MRS monitors and measures body chemistry, such as metabolism. MRS is a diagnostic tool for determination of many brain disorders, the degree of malignancy of tumors, and for evaluating metabolic disorders of the muscles and nervous system. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and positioned on a movable table, the provider identifies the area of abnormality or region of interest and places a special antenna or coil over or around the area to be imaged. He then moves the table into the magnetic field and takes images. He may inject contrast to enhance the images as needed. Then he creates and analyzes the MRS graph or spectrum arraying the types and quantity of chemicals in the brain or other organs. He compares the results with normal spectra and abnormal patterns for the interpretation. Terminology Magnetic resonance imaging or MRI: A diagnostic imaging technique that uses magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize body tissues to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy: A diagnostic imaging technique that uses a large, strong magnetic field and radio waves to measure the chemical composition of body tissues, instead of anatomic images, to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases; also known as nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, or NMR, and proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging. Tips When a provider performs both an MRI and MRS, report both the appropriate MRI code and the MRS code 76390. Check payer coverage for MRS. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. short_description: Echoencephalography, real time with image documentation (gray scale) (for determination of ventricular size, delineation of cerebral contents, and detection of fluid masses or other intracranial abnormalities), including A-mode encephalography as secondary component where indicated
lay_term: The provider performs a noninvasive diagnostic imaging technique, called echoencephalography, that uses ultrasound waves to examine, measure, and record the structures within the skull in real–time, meaning as the processes occur. The exam can diagnose intracranial abnormalities and conditions that cause a shift in the midline structure of the brain such as hemorrhage, fluid collection, masses, or other structural abnormalities. The provider may also take a one–dimensional recording of the electrical activity of the brain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and positioned, the provider positions the transducer, a device that converts electrical signals into ultrasound waves and ultrasound waves back into electrical impulses, against the head. He then guides the transducer over the head and sends an ultrasonic beam into the skull, and the reflected waves are captured as electrical impulses. When he obtains and images a satisfactory echo pattern, he displays the images on a monitor for immediate assessment and/or records the images for later interpretation. When indicated, the provider also measures the electrical activity of the brain, by placing electrodes on the scalp and recording the electric currents generated by the brain. Terminology A–mode, amplitude mode: A one–dimensional ultrasonic measurement. Echoencephalography: Imaging service that uses ultrasound waves to study intracranial structures and detect abnormalities and disease. Gray scale: Amount of energy a tissue absorbs represented in intensities of shades of gray. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high–frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. guidelines: Radiology Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All diagnostic ultrasound examinations require permanently recorded images with measurements, when such measurements are clinically indicated. For those codes whose sole diagnostic goal is a biometric measure (ie, 76514, 76516, and 76519), permanently recorded images are not required. A final, written report should be issued for inclusion in the patient's medical record. The prescription form for the intraocular lens satisfies the written report requirement for 76519. For those anatomic regions that have "complete" and "limited" ultrasound codes, note the elements that comprise a "complete" exam. The report should contain a description of these elements or the reason that an element could not be visualized (eg, obscured by bowel gas, surgically absent). If less than the required elements for a "complete" exam are reported (eg, limited number of organs or limited portion of region evaluated), the "limited" code for that anatomic region should be used once per patient exam session. A "limited" exam of an anatomic region should not be reported for the same exam session as a "complete" exam of that same region. Evaluation of vascular structures using both color and spectral Doppler is separately reportable. To report, see Noninvasive Vascular Diagnostic Studies (93880-93990). short_description: Ophthalmic ultrasound, diagnostic; corneal pachymetry, unilateral or bilateral (determination of corneal thickness) Notes: (Do not report 76514 in conjunction with 0402T)
lay_term: The provider uses conventional contact B scan imaging to measure the thickness of the cornea in one or both eyes. He then discards the high and low readings and averages the remaining measurements to determine the thickness of the cornea in microns. short_description: Ophthalmic biometry by ultrasound echography, A-scan

Explanation The provider performs A scan ultrasound, which uses echography, or high frequency sound waves, to provide one dimensional data on the structures of the eye. In this exam, the provider uses A scan ultrasound to measure from the cornea to the retina, for calculation of the axial eye length. After the patient is seated in the exam chair, and the provider instills a topical anesthetic into the eye, the provider instructs the patient to focus on a distant object to steady the patient’s eye. The provider then aligns the ultrasound probe on the cornea and directs a thin, sound beam in a straight line from the probe tip. The sound beam strikes each surface and bounces back into the probe tip, which converts each echo into a spike arising from a baseline that appears on a display screen for the provider’s review. short_description: Ophthalmic ultrasonic foreign body localization
lay_term: The provider uses ophthalmic ultrasound to locate a foreign body within the globe, or eyeball, which may be as a result of trauma or surgery. Explanation Ophthalmic ultrasound, also known as ocular echography, is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to examine the eye structure and diagnose disorders. B scan ultrasound, also known as bright scan, uses high frequency sound waves to provide a cross sectional, two dimensional view of the eye structure. It is very helpful for diagnosing retinal detachment, vitreous bleeding, tumors, or foreign bodies in the eye socket. An A scan ultrasound uses high frequency sound waves to provide one dimensional information of the eye structures. It helps in measuring the tissue thickness and the eye length. This diagnostic procedure determines the presence and location of intraocular foreign body or bodies or IOFBs within the eye. In this exam, the provider uses a standard contact B scan ultrasonography to locate a foreign body by placing the probe on the eye and transmitting an oscillating sound beam into the eye; the echoes that return are shown as a large number of dots that together form an image on a screen. The provider may then detect the presence and location of IOFBs, often following a track to the IOFB. The provider may also obtain additional information during the exam, including retinal and choroidal detachments, vitreous hemorrhage and posterior exit wounds that he also documents, as all the findings are useful to the decision on how to approach the case. Terminology Choroidal detachment: The middle vascular membrane that lies between the retina and the sclera, known as the choroid, becomes lifted from the sclera by an accumulation of eye fluid or blood. Localization: To determine the site or place of something such as an object, process, or lesion. Retinal detachment: Separation of the retina from the underlying layer of support tissue Vitreous hemorrhage: Leakage of blood into one of the many spaces formed within and around the clear gel that fills the space between the lens and the retina of the eyeball, known as the vitreous humor or vitreous body. short_description: Ultrasound, chest (includes mediastinum), real time with image documentation
lay_term: The provider uses ultrasound to evaluate the pleural spaces for the presence of fluid or masses of the chest, upper back, chest wall, or mediastinum. Explanation The provider positions the patient appropriately for the disease process or condition being investigated, such as sitting with arms extended for examination of a pleural effusion. The provider places acoustic gel on the patient’s skin in the area to be scanned. The provider then places and orients the probe in the best position to scan, for example, between the ribs, as ribs block transmission of ultrasound. The provider methodically moves the transducer longitudinally from one interspace to another to examine multiple interspaces for a comprehensive analysis of the target effusion or other condition. After completion of a general examination of the thorax, the provider may concentrate on an area of particular interest correctly identify structures and conditions. A chest ultrasound may include transverse, longitudinal, and oblique images of the chest wall with measurements of chest wall thickness. The provider reviews the images on the monitor and writes and places a report and images into to the patient’s chart and sends the same to the requesting physician. Terminology Longitudinally: Lengthwise, or along the length of the body or body site. Mediastinum: Tissues and organs between the lungs and situated between the breast bone in front, and the spine behind. Oblique: An angled view. Pleural effusion: A collection of fluid around the lungs. Pleural spaces: Area between the membranes that surround the lungs and the chest cavity, also called the pleural cavity. Transverse: Runs across the body. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Tips The provider need not examine and notate an examination of the mediastinum to report 76604, but you cannot report a mediastinum exam separately if the physician notes it during a chest ultrasound. If you are reporting only the physician’s interpretation for the radiology service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the radiology code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the radiology service, you would append modifier TC to the radiology code. Note, however, that payer policy may exempt hospitals from appending modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the radiology code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Additional Info In an ultrasound examination, a transducer, a device that converts high–frequency sound waves, both sends the signals and records the echoing waves. When the transducer is pressed against the skin, it directs a stream of inaudible, high–frequency sound waves into the body. As the sound waves bounce off the internal organs, fluids, and tissues, the sensitive microphone in the transducer records tiny changes in the sound's pitch and direction. A computer instantly measures and displaces these signature waves, which in turn creates a real–time picture on the monitor. The provider usually records these live images on videotape, and typically captures one or more frames of the moving pictures as still images. Read Less

short_description: Ultrasound, spinal canal and contents
lay_term: The provider uses sound waves to capture images of the entire spinal canal including the spinal cord, vertebrae, and intervertebral discs. The provider performs this service intraoperatively to identify and locate spinal tumors, small bony fragments, herniated disc material, or bullet fragments within the canal, or to guide surgical instruments to their target during the procedure. This exam also evaluates newborns and infants for various disorders. Explanation The provider positions the patient appropriately for the disease process or condition being investigated and aligns the ultrasound probe to appropriately direct the sound beam. The sound beam strikes each surface and bounces back into the probe tip, which converts the echoes into a picture that appears on a display screen for the provider’s review. In newborns and infants, the provider may examine the spinal canal in the midline longitudinal plane or the transverse plane. In an adult intraoperative procedure, the surgeon or radiologist uses a sterilized probe, or a probe prepared with a sterile cover or sheath, as the probe may be in direct contact with the organ or site. A provider may use ultrasound when he removes, or incises, all or part of the thin bony layer that covers and protects the spinal canal and spinal cord, a procedure called a laminotomy or laminectomy. He images the site in both longitudinal and transverse planes to visualize abnormalities, assesses how the operation is proceeding, and gauges the final outcome of the operation before finishing the surgery. The provider may also move the probe slowly and carefully to image the two planes during other spinal surgeries to locate a spinal tumor, guide an intraoperative biopsy, or ensure the completeness of a spinal lesion resection, removing the lesion from the spine. short_description: Ultrasound, pregnant uterus, real time with image documentation, fetal and maternal evaluation, after first trimester (> or = 14 weeks 0 days), transabdominal approach; each additional gestation (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 76810 in conjunction with 76805)
lay_term: In this add–on procedure, the provider performs a transabdominal ultrasound to examine each additional gestation sac, or fetus, after the first trimester. Explanation After performing an ultrasound examination of the first fetus, the provider performs another ultrasound during the same session, using a transabdominal approach, to examine each additional fetus, after the first trimester, or after the first 14 weeks of pregnancy. He applies gel to the ultrasound transducer head and places it over the patient’s abdomen. The provider then slowly moves the transducer over the mother’s abdomen. Ultrasound waves are high–frequency sound waves that travel through tissues of varying densities. The receiving unit or the monitor receives the sound waves after reflection and uses them to create images of the developing fetus and female pelvic structures. Use +76810 for ultrasound examination of each additional gestation after examination of the first fetus. Terminology Fetus: The term used for an unborn offspring, or baby, in the later stage of development before it is born. Gestation: The developmental period from conception to birth. Transabdominal: Through the abdomen or abdominal wall. Trimester: Three months period, most commonly seen during pregnancy. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high–frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Ultrasound transducer: A small hand–held device that resembles a microphone and attaches to an ultrasound scanner by a cord; the transducer sends out high–frequency sound waves into the body and then detects the returning echoes from the tissues in the body. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear–shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus, or womb, to the external genital opening, or introitus; also known as the birth canal. lay_term: In this add–on procedure, the provider uses either a transabdominal or transvaginal ultrasound to measure the fetal nuchal translucency, or the clear, fluid–filled space of the tissue at the back of a developing fetus's neck, for each additional fetus, during the first trimester. The aim of performing this ultrasound is to diagnose any abnormality or defect in the chromosomes of the fetus during development. Explanation A fetal nuchal ultrasound is a pregnancy ultrasound, which the provider performs during the first trimester to view any defect in the heart or chromosomes of the fetus. Nuchal translucency refers to the fluid, which is present at the back of the head and neck of the fetus, just underneath the skin, which is permeable to ultrasound waves. The definite measurement of the thickness of the fluid is known as a nuchal translucency measurement. It is measurable between 11 and 14 weeks gestation, and increase in the fluid is a sign of chromosomal abnormality. The provider uses either a transvaginal or transabdominal ultrasound. In a transabdominal approach, the provider applies a gel on the ultrasound transducer head and places the head on the patient's lower abdomen. The provider then slowly moves the transducer over the mother’s abdomen. In a transvaginal ultrasound, the provider places a protective disposable sheath, or covering, over a smaller transducer and applies gel on the transducer head. She then inserts the probe into the vagina and performs an internal ultrasound. A transvaginal approach has an advantage in that it gives clearer images of the fetus and the maternal organs. In either approach, the sound waves reflect through the tissues of different densities. The receiving unit receives these sound waves after reflection and uses them to create images of the nuchal translucency in the fetus. Use code +76814 when the provider measures the nuchal translucency of additional fetuses. Transabdominal: Through the abdomen or abdominal wall. Transvaginal: Through the vagina. Trimester: Three months period, most commonly seen during pregnancy. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Ultrasound transducer: A small hand–held device that resembles a microphone and attaches to an ultrasound scanner by a cord; the transducer sends out high–frequency sound waves into the body and then detects the returning echoes from the tissues in the body. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear–shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus, or womb, to the external genital opening, or introitus; also known as the birth canal. Codes 76811 and 76812 include all elements of codes 76805 and 76810 plus detailed anatomic evaluation of the fetal brain/ventricles, face, heart/outflow tracts and chest anatomy, abdominal organ specific anatomy, number/length/architecture of limbs and detailed evaluation of the umbilical cord and placenta and other fetal anatomy as clinically indicated. Report should document the results of the evaluation of each element described above or the reason for non-visualization. Code 76815 represents a focused "quick look" exam limited to the assessment of one or more of the elements listed in code 76815. Code 76816 describes an examination designed to reassess fetal size and interval growth or reevaluate one or more anatomic abnormalities of a fetus previously demonstrated on ultrasound, and should be coded once for each fetus requiring reevaluation using modifier 59 for each fetus after the first. Code 76817 describes a transvaginal obstetric ultrasound performed separately or in addition to one of the transabdominal examinations described above. For transvaginal examinations performed for non-obstetrical purposes, use code 76830. Section Specific Guideline All diagnostic ultrasound examinations require permanently recorded images with measurements, when such measurements are clinically indicated. For those codes whose sole diagnostic goal is a biometric measure (ie, 76514, 76516, and 76519), permanently recorded images are not required. A final, written report should be issued for inclusion in the patient's medical record. The prescription form for the intraocular lens satisfies the written report requirement for 76519. For those anatomic regions that have "complete" and "limited" ultrasound codes, note the elements that comprise a "complete" exam. The report should contain a description of these elements or the reason that an element could not be visualized (eg, obscured by bowel gas, surgically absent). If less than the required elements for a "complete" exam are reported (eg, limited number of organs or limited portion of region evaluated), the "limited" code for that anatomic region should be used once per patient exam session. A "limited" exam of an anatomic region should not be reported for the same exam session as a "complete" exam of that same region. Evaluation of vascular structures using both color and spectral Doppler is separately reportable. To report, see Noninvasive Vascular Diagnostic Studies (93880-93990). However, color Doppler alone, when performed for anatomic structure identification in conjunction with a real-time ultrasound examination, is not reported separately. Ultrasound guidance procedures also require permanently recorded images of the site to be localized, as well as a documented description of the localization process, either separately or within the report of the procedure for which the guidance is utilized. Use of ultrasound, without thorough evaluation of organ(s) or anatomic region, image documentation, and final, written report, is not separately reportable. Definitions A-mode implies a one-dimensional ultrasonic measurement procedure. M-mode implies a one-dimensional ultrasonic measurement procedure with movement of the trace to record amplitude and velocity of moving echo-producing structures. B-scan implies a two-dimensional ultrasonic scanning procedure with a two-dimensional display. Real-time scan implies a two-dimensional ultrasonic scanning procedure with display of both two-dimensional structure and motion with time. (To report diagnostic vascular ultrasound studies, see 93880-93990) (For focused ultrasound ablation treatment of uterine leiomyomata, see Category III codes 0071T, 0072T)

short_description: Doppler echocardiography, fetal, pulsed wave and/or continuous wave with spectral display; complete
lay_term: The provider performs a complete fetal Doppler echocardiography by pulsed or continuous sound waves with spectral display to assess blood flow in the fetus. Explanation The provider or sonographer (ultrasound technician) applies a gel to the ultrasound transducer and moves it over the pregnant patient's abdomen, pressing down gently on the transducer. The transducer sends high–frequency sound waves through the abdomen and picks up the echoes which it transmits to a computer that translates them into images. The procedure uses pulsed (intermittent) sound waves which allow measurement of blood flow velocities at a single point or over a small section. Alternatively, he may use continuous waves which allow blood velocity measurement over an entire line of interrogation. The provider may use both pulsed and continuous wave. Spectral display displays the images on a graph, with velocity along one axis and time along another; flow toward the transducer is shown above the baseline, while flow away is shown below the baseline. The physician performs this service to study the unborn baby's heart in much greater detail than is possible with a routine pregnancy ultrasound when the mother is at risk for giving birth to a baby with heart defects. Terminology Cardiovascular: Pertaining to the heart and blood vessels, that is, the circulatory system. Echocardiogram (Echo): The use of high–frequency sound waves or sonography (ultrasound) to create a two–dimensional image of the heart. Ultrasound: The use of high–frequency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Ultrasound transducer: A small hand–held device, resembling a microphone, that when placed on the skin or other tissue sends high–frequency sound waves through the tissues and detects their returning echoes to provide information about the underlying structures. Tips For a repeat or follow–up study, see 76828. If you are reporting only the physician’s interpretation for the radiology service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the radiology code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the radiology service, you would append modifier TC to the radiology code. Note, however, that payer policy may exempt hospitals from appending modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the radiology code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Read Less

short_description: Saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS), including color flow Doppler, when performed Notes: (For introduction of saline for saline infusion sonohysterography, use 58340)
lay_term: The provider performs an ultrasound examination during which he infuses saline into the uterus and may also use color flow Dopper to enhance imaging. Explanation The patient is placed in the lithotomy position after emptying her bladder. A vaginal speculum is inserted into the vagina. The cervix is prepped with Betadine (an antiseptic solution). A sonohysterographic catheter is then passed through the cervix and into the uterus. A 20 mL syringe containing sterile normal saline is attached to the catheter. Instillation of the sterile normal saline is begun slowly under direct sonographic visualization after the speculum is removed. The provider or ultrasound technician then applies conductive gel over a condom that has been placed over the transducer. The gel helps in the transmission of the sound waves. An ultrasound machine sends high–frequency sound waves through the probe. The provider then moves the transducer around inside the vagina, and images of the reproductive organs are displayed on a monitor. He may also employ color flow Doppler for enhanced imaging. At the conclusion of the procedure, the catheter and probe are removed and the saline is allowed to drain from the uterus. A hysterosonogram (also known as a saline ultrasound, saline sonogram, or saline infusion sonogram) is an ultrasound technique developed to better image the uterine cavity. It is useful for evaluating the endometrial lining in a patient with postmenopausal bleeding and for evaluating endometrial fibroids or tumors. Although it may be used in combination with hysterosalpingography in the evaluation of infertility, it is not the same thing as hysterosalpingography, which is a radiological imaging procedure in which contrast material is instilled into the uterus and fluoroscopy and plain X–rays are used to evaluate the endometrial cavity and fallopian tubes. lay_term: A pelvic ultrasound is a noninvasive procedure used to assess one or more pelvic structures, such as bladder, ovaries, uterus, cervix, and fallopian tubes in females and the bladder, prostate gland, and seminal vesicles in males. This helps in the transmission of the sound waves. An ultrasound machine sends high–frequency sound waves through a probe which is called transducer. The transducer is then pressed against the skin and moved over the area being studied. Use this code for a complete ultrasound to examine one or more, but not all, the pelvic organs. This procedure is usually performed to follow up or reevaluate findings on a previous ultrasound or to assess a limited number of structures in the pelvis. lay_term: The provider inserts an ultrasound probe into the rectum and performs a transrectal ultrasound to assess disorders of the prostate, rectum, and surrounding tissues. Explanation After appropriate preparation, the patient lies on his side with knees tucked up toward the chest. Sedation may be introduced. The provider inspects the anus and perianal area and may perform a digital rectal exam. The provider then gently inserts into the rectum the ultrasound transducer, which is sheathed in a plastic covering with gel covering the transducer and the tip of the plastic sheath. Once past the anal sphincter, he gently moves the transducer around to examine the base of the prostate and seminal vesicles. He examines the transition and peripheral zones of the prostate in the axial and sagittal planes. He identifies the urethra and verumontanum as well as the neurovascular structures. The provider measures prostate volume by imaging the transverse and anteroposterior dimensions at the estimated point of the widest transverse dimension in the axial plane and the longitudinal dimension in the sagittal plane just off the midline. He applies a formula, such as the ellipsoid volume formula (volume = height × width × length × 0.52) to the measurements to determine prostate volume. Once the examination is complete, the provider removes the ultrasound transducer from the rectum. Terminology Prostate: A small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder; it secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. Ultrasound: The use of high–frequency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. For the diagnostic ultrasound, you should report code 76872. Ultrasound guidance has a separate code (76942). You may also need to report a cyst aspiration code, such as 10160, depending on the nature of the procedure. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses ultrasound to examine the complete joint for any defect or abnormality. The image appears in real time on a monitor, and a permanent image with interpretation is placed in the patient's chart. Explanation The provider appropriately preps the patient and applies gel to the target area to enhance the connection between the tissues and the transducer head. The transducer produces sound waves that bounce off body tissues and make echoes, and then the transducer receives the echoes and sends them to a computer that uses them to create an image. The provider places the transducer head on the skin of the target joint and moves the transducer head to image the joint space and soft tissue structures around the joint. This is an exam of the complete joint. The image appears in real time on a monitor, and a permanent copy is made and documented in the medical record. guidelines: Radiology Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Code 76881 represents a complete evaluation of a specific joint in an extremity. Code 76881 requires ultrasound examination of all of the following joint elements: joint space (eg, effusion), peri-articular soft-tissue structures that surround the joint (ie, muscles, tendons, other soft-tissue structures), and any identifiable abnormality.
