short_description: Ultrasound, infant hips, real time with imaging documentation; dynamic (requiring physician or other qualified health care professional manipulation)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an ultrasound examination of the hips of an infant while manipulating the patient’s leg and hips during the procedure. This test helps detect any abnormality present in the hip such as developmental dysplasia of the hip, or DDH. Explanation Ultrasound of the hip is a noninvasive procedure that uses high frequency sound waves to evaluate the hips of an infant, and provides real time, two dimensional images of the hip. The provider performs the procedure using a standard B mode, or brightness mode, ultrasonic imager. The provider squeezes the knee moving the hip outward. He then applies gel on the ultrasound transducer head and places the head on the hip. The provider then slowly moves the transducer over the area. Sound waves from the ultrasound pass through tissues of varying densities. These sound waves reflect back to the receiving unit, which converts these waves into longitudinal, transverse, and oblique images of the hip. Terminology B mode or B scan ultrasound: Imaging technique using high frequency sound waves to provide a cross sectional, two dimensional view in gray scale imaging; also known as bright scan. Developmental dysplasia of the hip, or DDH:A dislocation of the hip joint that is present from birth. Dynamic: Imaging during movement or compression. Gray scale: Amount of energy a tissue absorbs represented in intensities of shades of gray; blacks, grays, and whites appear according to density and penetration, or absorption of X–rays. Longitudinal: In a lengthwise direction. Oblique: An angled view. Real time: Live imaging. Static: Delay in any movement. Transverse: Crossing a structure in an angular fashion. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Ultrasound transducer: A small hand held device that resembles a microphone and attaches to an ultrasound scanner by a cord; the transducer sends out high frequency sound waves into the body and then detects the returning echoes from the tissues in the body. short_description: Ultrasound guided compression repair of arterial pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistulae (includes diagnostic ultrasound evaluation, compression of lesion and imaging)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses ultrasound to assist with diagnosis and compression repair of an arterial pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistulae. Explanation Ultrasound is when the provider uses high–frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. In this procedure, the provider makes use of duplex scanning, which combines traditional ultrasound with Doppler, to diagnose the arterial pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistulae. He then plans the repair by compression. He applies compression at the neck of the pseudoaneurysm under real–time ultrasound guidance while still allowing blood flow through the supplying artery. He applies continuous pressure on the pseudoaneurysm until it gets thrombosed and leakage of blood stops completely. Or in a similar manner, he repairs the arteriovenous fistula by compressing it under ultrasound guidance and by blocking the blood flow to the damaged vessel, repeating for additional fistulae as needed. Finally, he again performs duplex ultrasound scanning to ensure the repair results are satisfactory. Terminology Arteriovenous fistula: Abnormal connection between artery and vein. Doppler: A technique to measure the flow of blood in a blood vessel. Pseudoaneurysm: Leakage of arterial blood from an artery resulting in formation of hematoma. short_description: Ultrasound guidance for vascular access requiring ultrasound evaluation of potential access sites, documentation of selected vessel patency, concurrent realtime ultrasound visualization of vascular needle entry, with permanent recording and reporting (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Do not report 76937 in conjunction with 33274, 33275, 36568, 36569, 36572, 36573, 36584, 36836, 36837, 37191, 37192, 37193, 37760, 37761, 76942, 0795T, 0796T, 0797T, 0798T, 0799T, 0800T, 0801T, 0802T, 0803T, 0823T, 0824T, 0825T) (Do not report 76937 in conjunction with 0505T, 0620T for ultrasound guidance for vascular access) (If extremity venous non-invasive vascular diagnostic study is performed separate from venous access guidance, see 93970, 93971)
lay_term: The provider uses ultrasound to help guide procedures requiring vascular access including central venous, peripheral venous, or arterial access procedures. Explanation Before the provider prepares the site for needle puncture; she uses ultrasound to choose the best site by evaluating the vessels for size, depth, course, surrounding structures, and any adjacent deviations from the norm. She then assesses a chosen vessel for patency, meaning that it is open and unobstructed, and looks for any other anatomic issues. The provider documents the sites she examines. Once the provider finalizes her selection, the patient is appropriated prepped and anesthetized. She places the probe in a sterile cover or sheath and uses ultrasound to determine the depth of the center of the intended vessel. She then visualizes the depression of the skin on the ultrasound monitor directly over the target vessel as the tip of the needle begins to penetrate the skin. She advances the needle in small increments checking the ultrasound screen to ensure she is maintaining the proper needle trajectory, or path. Once she passes the needle into the vessel, the provider uses ultrasound to confirm placement and to ensure it is not visible in adjacent vessels, and she records this position. lay_term: Ultrasonography uses sound waves of higher frequencies (above the normal hearing capacity of a healthy human, i.e., 20 kHz) to visualize inner organs. When the sound waves pass through the human body, they are reflected back at different speeds by the different types of tissues, e.g., bones, muscles, etc. These rebounding waves are captured and converted to images. While doing procedures such as a needle biopsy, the physician needs imaging guidance to know the exact location of the region to be biopsied and the accurate placement of the needle in that region. With the help of ultrasonography, the physician can move the needle inside the body to reach the tissue to be biopsied without causing damage to the surrounding tissues. short_description: Ultrasonic guidance for amniocentesis, imaging supervision and interpretation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs imaging supervision and interpretation for separately reportable amniocentesis, using ultrasound guidance. This invasive diagnostic procedure withdraws a sampling of amniotic fluid from the amniotic sac surrounding the fetus to test the fluid and fetal cells to detect birth defects. Explanation Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. In this procedure, the provider uses ultrasound guidance to insert a fine needle through a pregnant patient’s abdomen and into the uterus to obtain fluid from the amniotic sac surrounding the fetus. The provider begins by using the ultrasound probe prior to amniocentesis to scan the abdomen to identify the uterus, placenta, fetus, and to assess such factors as fetal viability, gestational age, amniotic fluid volume, and uterine cavity abnormalities or fibroids. She also uses the ultrasound to determine the most appropriate location to insert the needle. Once she identifies a site that has ample amniotic fluid and that is a safe distance away from the fetus, she marks the location on the patient’s skin. She gives the patient a local anesthetic, and the provider uses an antiseptic to clean the site. She places the ultrasound probe in a sterile cover or sheath and uses the ultrasound guidance as she inserts the needle through the patient’s abdominal and uterine walls into the pocket of amniotic fluid within the amniotic sac. She withdraws a small amount of fluid and sends it to the lab for testing. Tips When a patient is pregnant with twins, the provider may perform amniocentesis twice at the same encounter. short_description: Ultrasound, targeted dynamic microbubble sonographic contrast characterization (non-cardiac); initial lesion
lay_term: The provider injects the patient with contrast material consisting of lipid– or protein–coated microspheres filled with a gas core and performs targeted microbubble contrast–enhanced ultrasound examination to assess lesions suspicious for malignancy or to assess the blood flow in organs such as the liver and kidneys. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and lying on the examination table, the provider applies gel over the area to be examined and takes preliminary ultrasound images to compare with later images. He then injects the patient intravenously with lipid– or protein–coated microspheres filled with a gas core. This contrast material is heavier than air and can pass through microcapillaries enabling very sensitive ultrasound detection. After the contrast is injected and allowed to circulate for a few minutes, he records the average signal intensity of attached and circulating microbubbles. He then administers a high–powered ultrasound pulse to destroy the microbubbles that are attached to tissues. Again, after allowing the remaining microbubbles to circulate for a few seconds, he records the signal intensity of just the circulating microbubbles. The microbubbles dissipate shortly after the procedure is completed. Terminology Ultrasound: The use of high–frequency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Tips For each additional lesion with separate injection, report 76979. Read Less

short_description: Ultrasound, elastography; first target lesion
lay_term: The provider carries out ultrasound elastography of an initial suspicious lesion to help determine whether it is benign or malignant by measuring its return to normal shape after distortion by high–intensity ultrasound waves. Explanation The provider applies gel over the body area to be examined. He applies pressure over area of the suspected lesion, typically using the ultrasound probe, applies high–intensity ultrasound waves, and captures multiple images. He uses the images to measure the displacement of tissue and the amount of time it takes for the tissue to return to its normal shape. Finally, the provider uses various formulas to calculate the degree of displacement of the tissues being examined. Nonmalignant tumors display more elasticity than cancerous tumors, and fibrotic (thickened and scarred) tissue shows less elasticity and is slower to resume its normal shape than normal tissues. Terminology Benign: Not malignant, generally treatable or not needing treatment. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass, benign or cancerous. Ultrasound: The use of high–frequency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Tips For ultrasound elastography of each additional lesion, see +76983. For ultrasound elastography of an organ to assess the condition of its functional tissue, see 76981. Read Less

lay_term: The provider uses fluoroscopic guidance to place a needle for biopsy, aspiration, injection, or localization of a device to detect any lesions in any area of the body, except for the spine, or to identify the level and approach for initial needle placement. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and draped, the patient is placed under the fluoroscope in the supine or prone position. The provider then places the tip of the needle or catheter at the introduction site. Using fluoroscopy to guide him, he inserts the needle into the desired region, advancing it slowly to the designated location inside the body. Once the needle reaches the appropriate level, he injects contrast material at the site to confirm the proper needle placement. The provider then may perform diagnostic or therapeutic procedures via the needle or catheter, such as localizing or identifying a specific area of interest or location of a structure in the body, taking samples of tissue or withdrawing small amounts of cells or fluid to send for further analysis, or injecting a substance to treat a condition such as acute or chronic pain. Fluoroscopy displays live X–ray images on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Terminology Aspiration: Removal of fluid, gas, or other material through a tube attached to a suction device, often combined with irrigation, the instillation of fluid to clean a wound or to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen or stomach. Biopsy: Process of taking one or more tissue samples through the biopsy forceps from a living body for diagnostic purposes. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Global value ZZZ: Identifies the service as an add–on code, or a code related to another service, which is always included in the global period of the other service. Injection: Use of a syringe to forcibly instill a liquid substance into tissues, vessels, or tumors; the instilling of a medicinal substance using various routes that include subcutaneous, below the skin, intravenous, within a vein, or intramuscular, into a muscle, among others; also, excessive accumulation of blood in an area causing redness. Do not report with arthrography radiological supervision and interpretation codes. If the provider uses fluoroscopic guidance for placement of a needle or catheter tip in the spine or paraspinous region, use 77003. There may be rare instances where one provider supervises the radiology service and another provider interprets it. According to Medicare guidelines, each provider should report the radiology code and append modifier 52 (Reduced services). Each should also append modifier 26 to the code to indicate they are reporting only the professional portion of the service. If you are reporting only the technical component for the radiology service, you would append modifier TC to the radiology code. Note, however, that payer policy may exempt hospitals from appending modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. short_description: Computed tomography guidance for placement of radiation therapy fields Notes: (For placement of interstitial device[s] for radiation therapy guidance, see 31627, 32553, 49411, 55876)
lay_term: With the patient lying still on the examination table, the table moves through middle of the round CT scanner. The X–ray machine in the circular scanner produces narrow beams of X–rays (1–10 mm of thickness) that pass through specific parts of the patient's body. Different tissues of the human body absorb different amounts of X–rays. The electronic ray detectors detect the amount of radiation absorbed into the body. A special computer program processes the acquired data to create two–dimensional cross–sectional images of the targeted anatomical site which are displayed on computer monitor. This image is interpreted by a radiation oncologist or other specialist physician who can determine the tissue's condition (normal or diseased). In case of malignancy, the physician can determine the volume of the treatment field where the radiation needs to be applied, and also the healthy tissue area which should be protected from radiation. Explanation The imaging technologist instructs the patient to lie down on the examination table. Straps are used to keep the patient still during the examination, as body movement may cause inaccurate image recording. Sometimes a contrast material is injected at the site of imaging for better visibility of the internal organs. The CT scanner is a large box–like machine with a tunnel at the center. The examination table moves in and out through the tunnel. During the actual scanning process, the X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around the table, at a speed of approximately 1 rotation per second. The X–ray tubes produce narrow fan–shaped beams that pass through the specific target organ and hit the X–ray detectors. The technologist controls the entire process from an adjacent room. A computer terminal processes the raw data and produces clear two–dimensional images of the anatomy. The cross–sectional images or "image slices" are then examined by the specialist physician to determine the diseased tissue area and the area to which radiation is to be applied. This CT imaging for radiation therapy field determination also helps in determining the normal tissues around the treatment area that need to be blocked from irradiation. The entire CT imaging process takes about 30 minutes to complete. The patient is released once the technician instructs him to do so after verifying the image quality. Terminology Computed tomography (CT): An imaging procedure in which an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer–generated three–dimensional image of the inside of an object from a large series of two–dimensional X–ray images taken around a single axis of rotation; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Tomography: Image reconstruction of two– and three–dimensional objects through the use of any kind of penetrating wave; the word "tomography" comes from the Greek word "tomos" meaning "slice" or "section" and "graphe" meaning "drawing." short_description: Computed tomography, bone mineral density study, 1 or more sites, axial skeleton (eg, hips, pelvis, spine)
lay_term: Computed tomography (CT) is also known as CAT (computerized axial tomography), CTAT (computerized transaxial tomography), and digital axial tomography (DAT). It is a powerful noninvasive evaluation technique for producing 2D and 3D cross–sectional images of the body structures, including the bones. This CT scan study on the bones is used to evaluate diseases of bone and/or the responses of bone diseases to treatment. The studies assess bone mass or density associated with such diseases as osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and renal osteodystrophy. Various single or combined methods of measurement may be required to diagnose bone disease, monitor the course of bone changes with disease progression, or monitor the course of bone changes with therapy. Explanation Before an exam is performed the physician provides a contrast material (either IV or oral) to the patient. The patient is asked to lie down on the CT table, and straps and pillows are used for further support and positioning. The table is moved inside the scanner; the movement of table is controlled by the physician. Multiple narrow beams of X–rays are shot around the target bone and a special imaging program is used to produce thin slices or cross–sectional views of the target bone tissues. During this scanning procedure the patient is instructed to stay still and asked to hold his breath. Once the examination is completed the result is verified by the physician. A CT bone mineral study of one or more sites on the axial skeleton, e.g., on the hips, pelvis, or spine, is reported with CPT® code 77078. Terminology Computed tomography (CT): An imaging procedure in which an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer–generated three–dimensional image of the inside of an object from a large series of two–dimensional X–ray images taken around a single axis of rotation; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Tips Code it only once, even if more than one body site (bones) are examined in a single sitting. The code descriptor itself has provision to bill for the service performed on multiple sites of the axial skeleton. Read Less

short_description: Magnetic resonance (eg, proton) imaging, bone marrow blood supply
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses magnetic resonance imaging to study and evaluate the bone marrow blood supply. Explanation Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, uses magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize body tissues to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. In this procedure, the provider places the patient within an MRI scanner, which forms a strong magnetic field around the area to be imaged. MRI detects signals based on water content and local magnetic properties of a particular body area in a way that distinguishes one tissue from another. MRI is preferred for characterizing normal and abnormal bone marrow because of MRI’s ability to distinguish fat from other tissues. As a result, the provider can identify hematologic disorders resulting in alterations of the normal cellular and fatty marrow distribution. The MRI pattern of bone marrow can help in identifying disease processes that induces diffuse changes in bone marrow. MRI can also detect when cancerous cells slowly replace normal marrow, known as diffuse bone marrow infiltration. short_description: Therapeutic radiology treatment planning; complex
lay_term: The provider decides the location and the number of ports (the points for the radiation beams to enter the body), the design and location of the shielding blocks, and the modes of therapy (e.g., arc therapy or brachytherapy). The treatment may involve using either a single mode or a combination of different modes of therapy. Explanation A complex simulation–aided field setting which provides a complex geometric shape of a tumor specially in case of three or more malignant regions that need to be addressed. This requires a lot of complex planning and customization of the therapy to get maximum impact on the tumors while minimizing the damage to the healthy tissues that might come in the way of the radiation beams. The planning involves field setting for multiple modes of radiation therapy (such as tangential ports, rotation, or arc therapy), complex blocking (such as hemibody or inverted Y), brachytherapy, and arc therapy. It may also require designing of shielding blocks to be used to protect the healthy tissues. Radiation therapy is one of the most effective treatment methods for cancerous tumors. But it has its negative sides. Radiation can cause damage to the healthy cells of the body. Therefore, radiation therapy involves thorough planning of the dosage, the method, and the duration of the treatment, taking into consideration the size and location of the tumor. The treatment is aimed at destroying the malignant tumor without causing damage to the surrounding healthy tissues and organs. Read Less

short_description: Therapeutic radiology simulation-aided field setting; simple Notes: Simulation is the process of defining relevant normal and abnormal target anatomy, and acquiring the images and data necessary to develop the optimal radiation treatment process for the patient. If a simulation does not meet any of these criteria, the complexity is defined by the number of treatment areas: one treatment area is simple, two treatment areas are intermediate, and three or more treatment areas are complex. A treatment area is a contiguous anatomic location that will be treated with radiation therapy. Generally, this includes the primary tumor organ or the resection bed and the draining lymph node chains, if indicated. An example is a breast cancer patient for whom a single treatment area could be the breast alone or the breast, adjacent supraclavicular fossa, and internal mammary nodes. In some cases, a patient might receive radiation therapy to more than one discontinuous anatomic location. An example would be a patient with multiple bone metastases in separate sites (eg, femur and cervical spine); in this case, each distinct and separate anatomic site to be irradiated is a separate treatment area. short_description: Therapeutic radiology simulation-aided field setting; complex
lay_term: Before starting radiation therapy, a physician needs to know the location and size of the cancerous tumor, the radiation doses required to treat the tumor, and the positioning of the radiation beams to target the tumor. With the help of imaging and computerized reconstruction techniques, the physician creates a simulated field that closely resembles the location and size of the tumor in the body. The CT or MRI data of the patient is fed into a simulator that recreates the image of the tumor and its surrounding area. With the help of the simulator, the physician decides the ports where the radiation beams should enter the body so as to hit the tumor with maximum accuracy. Explanation A complex simulation–aided field setting provides a complex geometric shape of a tumor especially in case of three or more malignant regions that need to be addressed. This requires a lot of complex planning and customization of the therapy to get maximum impact on the tumors while minimizing the damage to the surrounding healthy tissues. The treatment may involve field setting for multiple modes of radiation therapy (such as tangential ports, rotation, or arc therapy), complex blocking (such as hemibody or inverted Y), brachytherapy, and arc therapy. It may also require designing shielding blocks to be used to protect the healthy tissues. Read Less

short_description: 3-dimensional radiotherapy plan, including dose-volume histograms
lay_term: Computer–generated radiographic reconstruction and volumetric dose calculation are used to improve accuracy of external beam radiation administration. Documentation may include 3D volume reconstruction, dose distribution, and dose volume histograms, a summary of 3D dose calculations in graph form. Explanation The provider uses fused data sets, i.e., imaging, to outline the patient's target volumes. The clinical target volume is based on adding a small area around the visible tumor, called the gross tumor volume, in case the disease has spread at a level that is not yet seen on imaging. The provider defines these volumes based on tumor location and surrounding anatomy, considering a large set of images. Planning target volumes, PTVs, are then added. PTV is a concept that allows for planning and treatment delivery uncertainties with a goal of ensuring the radiotherapy is delivered to the CTV. A patient may require multiple PTVs. Based on tumor location, the provider identifies the organs at risk, called ORs. He may add a margin around the ORs to minimize any radiation dose to a specified, acceptable level. The provider reviews the 3D computer dosimetry calculation provided by the physicist and dosimetrist, and then the three work together to adjust the plan to maximize treatment while minimizing damage to healthy tissue. Creating the final plan may take several attempts. Read Less

lay_term: Intensity modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) uses advanced computer technology to deliver very precise radiation beams that target and destroy the cancerous cells while avoiding the surrounding healthy tissue. With the help of three–dimensional computed tomography (CT) and a computer–controlled delivery system, multiple radiation beams of varying intensity are directed at the tumor from different angles. This reduces the risk of exposure for the healthy tissues that might come in the way of the beam as the intensity and angle of each beam can be adjusted with the help of the computerized delivery system. IMRT is widely used for treatment of cancerous tumors of the head, neck, prostate, lung, GI tract, thyroid, and breast. Explanation The physician plans an intensity modulated radiotherapy with the help of a computerized delivery system. The plan considers the location of the tumor, critical organs/tissues surrounding the tumor, the dose needed, numbers as well as angles of beams to be directed to cause maximum damage to the tumor while protecting the surrounding organs. The physician makes modifications to the delivery angle and beam intensity until the best possible configuration is made. Read Less

short_description: Teletherapy isodose plan; simple (1 or 2 unmodified ports directed to a single area of interest), includes basic dosimetry calculation(s)
lay_term: The provider arranges one or two parallel opposed treatment ports to achieve the isodose beam arrangement for external beam radiation therapy. Isodose means a radiation dose of equal intensity applied to a treatment field in the body. The provider also calculates the right dose on the basis of the type and stage of the cancer. Explanation The provider performs teletherapy isodose planning, where he plots lines to achieve equal intensity of radiation dose to a given treatment field, either by hand or by computer calculation. He calculates the right dose and method of radiation therapy based on the type and the stage of the cancer being treated. The provider uses various factors to calculate the dose and determine the optimal angle to place the port and to ensure equal intensity of radiation distribution over the treatment area. The provider expresses the dose levels in percentages within the target area and calculates the dosage to surrounding tissues. He places one or two unmodified ports, parallel and opposite to target a common treatment area. Terminology Dosimetry: Measurement of the radiation dose that the body receives and absorbs. External beam radiation: Treatment with high energy X–ray beams from a radiation source outside the body. Inhomogeneity: Elements of same kind and nature. Nonionizing radiation: Very low frequency electromagnetic radiation; radiation frequency, beam intensity, and duration exposure factor into how much energy tissue exposed to nonionizing radiation will absorb. Port: A point of entry of treatment. Radiation therapy: Application of high frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. Tangential port: Point of entry of treatment from which multiple lines of radiations diverge. Teletherapy: A type of radiotherapy that directs a beam of radiation from outside the body at cancerous tissue inside the body. Explanation The provider performs brachytherapy isodose planning to plot the radiation distribution around the brachytherapy source and expose the tumor area to the radiation while protecting the surrounding tissue from unwanted radiation exposure. He calculates the right dose based on the type and the stage of the cancer being treated. He plots the lines of equal radiation dose to the target area and notes the dosage to the surrounding tissues. This process includes complex planning using over 10 sources of radiation or over 12 channels for afterloading. Terminology Afterloading: Placing catheters, which are subsequently loaded with radioactive substance, at the treatment site. Brachytherapy: Placement of a radiation source inside the body near the cancer site to treat the tumor effectively. Dosimetry: Measurement of the radiation dose that the body receives and absorbs. Tips The code 77318 includes calculation of dose, so do not also report code 73000, Basic radiation dosimetry calculation, central axis depth dose calculation, TDF, NSD, gap calculation, off axis factor, tissue inhomogeneity factors, calculation of nonionizing radiation surface and depth dose, as required during course of treatment, only when prescribed by the treating physician. For simple brachytherapy planning, use code 77316, Brachytherapy isodose plan; simple, calculations made from one to four sources, or remote afterloading brachytherapy, one channel, includes basic dosimetry calculations. For intermediate brachytherapy planning, use code 77317, Brachytherapy isodose plan; intermediate, calculations made from five to 10 sources, or remote afterloading brachytherapy, two to12 channels, includes basic dosimetry calculations. lay_term: In this service, the radiation oncology provider plans for a special beam consideration such as electrons, which are heavy particles to treat a complex tumor. Special teletherapy port plans often are electron beam plans because the irradiation with an electron beam requires a high level of care. Providers most commonly use electron beam therapy for superficial skin lesions. Other particle beams may also be used by the provider like photons for hemibody radiation. The provider plans the selection of the special beam particles and calculates the dosage to be administered through the ports. Terminology Radiation oncology: Radiation oncology, also called radiotherapy, applies high–frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. short_description: Treatment devices, design and construction; simple (simple block, simple bolus)
lay_term: The provider participates in the design, construction, and selection of simple treatment devices such as a simple block or simple bolus. Providers use these devices for proper dose delivery to the tumor and protection of nearby healthy tissues. Explanation The provider selects, designs, and or constructs simple specialized devices such as simple blocks and simple boluses to minimize the amount of radiation that is delivered to normal tissue while maximizing the radiation dose to the tumor site. Blocks are treatment devices made up of the alloy Cerrobend®, which has a special radiation–absorbing property. A bolus is additional material, such as a flat piece of rubberlike material, used when treating uneven areas of a patient, such as a nose. Providers use the bolus to make up for missing tissue or to provide a buildup of dosage to the skin surface. Simple devices may be prefabricated. Terminology Radiotherapy: The application of high–frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. Tips This code has both professional and technical components, so be sure to append modifier 26, Professional component, when reporting only the provider's services. Documentation for the professional component typically includes the provider's judgment on the device selection and positioning. short_description: Continuing medical physics consultation, including assessment of treatment parameters, quality assurance of dose delivery, and review of patient treatment documentation in support of the radiation oncologist, reported per week of therapy
lay_term: This code is for reporting ongoing medical physics consultation. When a patient is undergoing radiation treatment for a particular span of time with a number of therapy sessions every week, the medical physicist needs to look into the ongoing treatment documentation. This service is usually reported weekly once, after a full week's therapy (generally five treatment sessions) is delivered. Explanation Usually a patient undergoing radiation therapy needs to attend five therapy sessions per week. The radiation oncologist along with the dosimetrist determines the dose of radiation to be applied, designs blocks and molds for proper delivery of radiation, interprets the obtained data after sessions, and documents the result. The radiologist performs the dose delivery procedure. This entire process of radiation therapy and its treatment plan needs a sort of verification and review on a weekly basis. The medical physicist oversees and validates the entire process plan, usually once in every week, after five treatment sessions. The medical physicist's service includes the following: Reviewing the patient treatment chart received from various members of patient management team. Checking the data to ensure that the patient received proper dosage of radiation. Reviewing patient positioning, machine setup, and effective utilization of devices such as molds, blocks, linear accelerators, etc. Assessing the safety measurements and other treatment parameters. Performing a final chart check and validation of the week–long treatment. Tips Continuing medical physics consultation (CPT® code 77336) is reported "per week of therapy". CPT® 77336 cannot be reported separately when the service is part of the IMRT planning process (CPT® 77301) Read Less

short_description: Multi-leaf collimator (MLC) device(s) for intensity modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), design and construction per IMRT plan Notes: (Do not report 77338 in conjunction with 77385 for compensator based IMRT) (Do not report 77338 more than once per IMRT plan) (For immobilization in IMRT treatment, see 77332-77334)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider participates in the design and construction of one or more multi–leaf collimator, MLC, devices for intensity modulated radiation therapy, IMRT. IMRT is a radiotherapy technique that varies the strength of the radiotherapy beams to match the size, shape, and position of the tumor, minimizing the damage to healthy tissue. Explanation IMRT is a radiotherapy technique that varies the strength of the radiotherapy beams to match the size, shape, and position of the tumor, maximizing the effectiveness of the treatment and minimizing the damage to healthy tissue. In this device service, the provider participates in the design and construction of a multi–leaf collimator device, abbreviated as MLC. This is a specialized computer–controlled device with as many as 120 tungsten fingers or leaves inside the linear accelerator. This device varies the strength of the radiotherapy beam to match the size, shape, and position of the tumor. The provider designs the MLC device based on the IMRT plan. Terminology Linear accelerator: A machine that is capable of producing high energy X–rays or electrons forming radiation beam. Radiation oncology: Radiation oncology, also called radiotherapy, applies high–frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. short_description: Radiation treatment delivery, stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS), complete course of treatment of cranial lesion(s) consisting of 1 session; multi-source Cobalt 60 based
lay_term: This code represents the technical component of stereotactic radiosurgery, in which a provider uses a three–dimensional coordinate system to locate small targets or lesions inside the brain and destroys them using externally generated ionized radiation. He uses a multi–source Cobalt 60 system as a source of radiation that generates high energy gamma rays. Explanation This code represents the technical component of a procedure in which the provider identifies the target area of the brain using the stereotactic method. This method uses previously taken CT or MRI images imported into a computer system to provide three–dimensional images of the brain. The goal of stereotactic radiosurgery is to destroy the target tissue while preserving adjacent normal tissue. The provider places the patient on a treatment table and uses the robotic arm controlled by computer that focuses directly on the head. He then uses a multi–source cobalt 60 system as a source of radiation to destroy one or more targets inside the brain. A multisource cobalt 60 system consists of 201 separate cobalt–60 sources arranged in a steel shell capable of producing radiation beams that intersect on the target. He performs the complete treatment in one session, and he may destroy more than one brain lesion in the same session. Terminology Radiation oncology: Radiation oncology, also called radiotherapy, applies high–frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. Tips Report 77371 only once regardless of the number of brain lesions treated in the same session. Code 77371 represents the technical component of the service only, so you should not append modifier 26 or TC. The provider performing radiation treatment management for this service should report 77432, which covers services like clinical treatment planning, administration of treatment, and overall case management. short_description: Stereotactic body radiation therapy, treatment delivery, per fraction to 1 or more lesions, including image guidance, entire course not to exceed 5 fractions Notes: (Do not report 77373 in conjunction with 77385, 77386, 77401, 77402, 77407, 77412) (For single fraction cranial lesion[s], see 77371, 77372)
lay_term: This code represents the technical component of a procedure in which the provider performs stereotactic body radiation therapy. The therapy uses a three–dimensional coordinate system to locate small targets or lesions inside the body, other than the brain and spinal cord, and destroys them with precision using externally generated ionized radiation. This code covers a single fraction of a course of up to five fractions. Explanation Stereotactic body radiation therapy is a type of radiation therapy in which the provider delivers a few very high doses of radiation to small, well–defined tumors inside the body. This code represents treatment delivery, which is the technical component, of a procedure in which the provider identifies the target area inside the body using the stereotactic method. In this method, the provider uses previously taken CT or MRI images imported into a computer system that provides three–dimensional images of internal body structure. He performs fractionated radiation treatment, which allows spreading the total dose out over time. The goal of using fractionated radiation treatment is to allow the normal cells time to recover, while tumor cells are generally less efficient in repair between fractions. He may destroy one or more lesion per fraction and does not exceed five fractions in a single therapy course. Terminology Radiation oncology: Radiation oncology, also called radiotherapy, applies high–frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. Tips Report this code per fraction. The provider performing radiation treatment management for this service should report 77435, which covers services like managing treatment, making adjustments based on patient movement, and assessing imaging used for localization. guidelines: Radiology Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Following dosimetry calculations, there are a number of alternative methods to deliver external radiation treatments, which are described with specific CPT® codes: X-ray (photon), including conventional and intensity modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) beams; Electron beams; Neutron beams; Proton beams. All treatment delivery codes are reported once per treatment session. The treatment delivery codes recognize technical-only services and contain no physician work (the professional component). In contrast, the treatment management codes contain only the professional component. Radiation treatment delivery with conventional X-ray or electron beams is assigned levels of complexity based on the number of treatment sites and complexity of the treatment fields, blocking, wedges, and physical or virtual tissue compensators. A simple block is straight-edged or an approximation of a straight edge created by a multileaf collimator (MLC). Energy of the megavoltage (>/= 1 MeV) beam does not contribute to complexity. Techniques such as treating a field-in-field to ensure dose homogeneity reflect added complexity. Energies below the megavoltage range may be used in the treatment of skin lesions. Superficial radiation energies (up to 200 kV) may be generated by a variety of technologies and should not be reported with megavoltage (77402, 77407, 77412) for surface application. Do not report clinical treatment planning (77261, 77262, 77263), treatment devices (77332, 77333, 77334), isodose planning (77306, 77307, 77316, 77317, 77318), physics consultation (77336), or radiation treatment management (77427, 77431, 77432, 77435, 77469, 77470, 77499) with 77401, 0394T, or 0395T. When reporting 77401 alone, evaluation and management, when performed, may be reported with the appropriate E/M codes. Intensity modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) uses computer-based optimization techniques with non-uniform radiation beam intensities to create highly conformal dose distributions that can be delivered by a radiotherapy treatment machine. A number of technologies, including spatially and temporally modulated beams, cylindrical beamlets, dynamic MLC, single or multiple fields or arcs, or compensators, may be used to generate IMRT. The complexity of IMRT may vary depending on the area being treated or the technique being used. Image guided radiation therapy (IGRT) may be used to direct the radiation beam and to reflect motion during treatment. A variety of techniques may be used to perform this guidance including imaging (eg, ultrasound, CT, MRI, stereoscopic imaging) and non-imaging (eg, electromagnetic or infrared) techniques. Guidance may be used with any radiation treatment delivery technique and is typically used with IMRT delivery. IMRT delivery codes include the technical component of guidance or tracking, if performed. Because only the technical portion of IGRT is bundled into IMRT, the physician involvement in guidance or tracking may be reported separately. When guidance is required with conventional radiation treatment delivery, both the professional and technical components are reported because neither component of guidance is bundled into conventional radiation treatment delivery services. The technical and professional components of guidance are handled differently with each radiation delivery code depending on the type of radiation being administered. The Radiation Management and Treatment Table is provided for clarity. Definitions Radiation Treatment Delivery, megavoltage (>/= 1 MeV), any energy Simple: All of the following criteria are met (and none of the complex or intermediate criteria are met): single treatment area, one or two ports, and two or fewer simple blocks. Intermediate: Any of the following criteria are met (and none of the complex criteria are met): 2 separate treatment areas, 3 or more ports on a single treatment area, or 3 or more simple blocks. Complex: Any of the following criteria are met: 3 or more separate treatment areas, custom blocking, tangential ports, wedges, rotational beam, field-in-field or other tissue compensation that does not meet IMRT guidelines, or electron beam. IMRT, any energy, includes the technical services for guidance. Simple: Any of the following: prostate, breast, and all sites using physical compensator based IMRT. Complex: Includes all other sites if not using physical compensator based IMRT. short_description: Radiation treatment delivery, >=1 MeV; simple Notes: (Do not report 77402 in conjunction with 77373)
lay_term: This code represents the technical component of a procedure in which the provider delivers radiation to a treatment area using greater than or equal to a 1 MeV energy level. The treatment involves a single treatment area; one or two ports; and zero, one, or two simple blocks. A block shields healthy tissue from radiation. Explanation This code represents only the technical component of simple level radiation treatment delivery, a procedure in which the provider places the patient on a table and delivers a radiation beam to the targeted body area using an external source of radiation. The provider may use various techniques to deliver the radiation, such as external beam radiotherapy which employs a linear accelerator that produces a high energy external radiation beam that pierces the tissue and dispenses the radiation dose deep within the areas where the cancer exists. The machine can generate radiation at different energy levels. The provider treats the area using greater than or equal to 1 MeV energy level, or one million electron volts, an indication of the amount of radiation energy delivered. short_description: Intensity modulated radiation treatment delivery (IMRT), includes guidance and tracking, when performed; simple Notes: (To report professional component [PC] of guidance and tracking, use 77387 with modifier 26)
lay_term: The provider uses computer designed mapping and physical compensator to deliver precise, high intensity radiation doses to a malignant tumor or specific areas within the tumor while minimizing the dose to surrounding normal tissues. He determines the treatment delivery based upon tumor shape and CT images along with computerized dose calculations. Providers use this type of radiation therapy to treat cancers like breast or prostate cancer. Explanation The provider begins the treatment by identifying the tumor using image guidance, typically computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging. He marks the patient’s skin with a special ink to specify the target location. He then uses a computer to calculate the optimal dose of the radiation to target the tumor site. He uses a physical compensator to modify the radiation beam so as to control the amount of cumulative radiation dose within the target and the acceptable radiation dose limits for the surrounding normal tissues. Terminology Computed tomography, or CT: An imaging procedure in which X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Image guided, imaging guidance: Use of live or real time X–ray imaging or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. Intensity modulated radiation therapy, or IMRT: A technology in radiation oncology that delivers radiation more precisely and with higher intensity to the tumor while relatively sparing the surrounding normal tissues. Linear accelerator: A medical linear accelerator produces the photons, or X–rays, used in IMRT; it delivers multiple beams of radiation to the tumor from various angles; a dynamic multileaf collimator, or MLC, controls and varies the radiation intensity of each beam according to the treatment plan. Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI: Use of magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize body tissues to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Prostate: Small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males; secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass, benign or cancerous. Tips For intensity modulated radiation treatment delivery using a medical linear accelerator and a multileaf collimator, or MLC, instead of a physical compensator, use code 77386, Intensity modulated radiation treatment delivery, or IMRT, includes guidance and tracking, when performed; complex. You may report the professional component using the 26 modifier for guidance and tracking when reporting this code. Read Less

short_description: High energy neutron radiation treatment delivery, 1 or more isocenter(s) with coplanar or non-coplanar geometry with blocking and/or wedge, and/or compensator(s)
lay_term: This code represents the technical component of a procedure in which the provider delivers high energy neutron radiation treatment to one or more isocenters. An isocenter is a common focus point of all radiation beams. He may use either coplanar or non–coplanar geometry radiation with blocking, wedge, and/or compensators. Explanation High energy neutron radiation therapy uses high energy neutron particles to destroy cancer cells and to slow down their growth. This code represents treatment delivery, which is the technical component of a procedure in which the provider treats one or more isocenters using high energy neutron radiation. He may use a coplanar or non–coplanar geometry of radiation. In coplanar radiation geometry, all the rays lie in the same plane, which is opposite to the pattern of rays in non–coplanar. He may also use blocks, a wedge, and/or a compensator to limit exposure of healthy tissue to the radiation and to maximize the radiation to the tumor area. Providers use neutron therapy to treat resistant cancers that providers cannot treat by conventional radiation treatment. High energy neutron radiation damages the tumor cell by nuclear interaction and limits the cells’ ability to repair themselves. Providers use this type of radiation to treat large tumors. The treatment does not depend on the presence of oxygen in the cell, unlike low energy radiation. In neutron radiation treatment, the required dose is one–third of that for conventional radiation because of the neutron radiation’s better biological effectiveness. Terminology Block: A lead alloy structure that protects the normal tissue from the effects of radiation. Compensator: A solid device attached to the linear accelerator; it shapes the radiation beam passing through it in a way that it provides the maximum dose to the tumor and minimizes the exposure of healthy tissues. Radiation oncology: Radiation oncology, also called radiotherapy, applies high–frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. Wedge: A radiation beam modifying device that ensures that the radiation is concentrated to the tumor area only. Read Less

short_description: Radiation treatment management, 5 treatments
lay_term: Radiation therapy utilizes ionizing radiation beams that are directed at cancerous cells in order to destroy them. The radiation, damages the DNA (the genetic material) in the cell, thus preventing further growth of the cancerous cells. Though there is the risk of damage to the normal cells, the risk is minimized through the use of highly advanced equipment that pinpoint the radiation beam to the cancerous cells and only the immediate surrounding healthy cells to eliminate any risk of regrowth. Radiation therapy can be successfully used in the treatment of most types of cancers including malignant tumors of different organs, lymphomas, leukemia and certain non–malignant conditions. Radiation therapy can be done externally (external radiation therapy) or internally (brachytherapy). In external radiation therapy, the source of the radiation remains outside the body. However, in brachytherapy, the radiation source or implant is inserted and placed internally near the cancerous cells. Explanation Radiation therapy can extend for up to five sessions in which the physician or oncologist schedules the treatment plan and takes care of the doses and duration of each session. The physician also monitors the effect of the treatment in order to adjust specific doses and medications to treat the patient. Tips The professional services furnished during treatment management typically consist of: 1. Review of port films 2. Review of dosimetry, dose delivery, and treatment parameters 3. Review of patient treatment set–up 4. Examination of patient for medical evaluation and management (e.g., assessment of the patient's response to treatment, coordination of care and treatment, review of imaging and/or lab test results) Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider manages the complete course of stereotactic body radiotherapy treatment in which he uses a three–dimensional coordinate system to locate small targets or lesions inside the body except the brain and spinal cord. The provider identifies the target area inside the body using the stereotactic method in which previously taken CT or MRI images are imported into a computer system that provides three dimensional images of internal body structure. He performs fractionated radiation treatment, with the total dose spread out over time. The goal of using fractionated radiation treatment is to allow the normal cells time to recover, while tumor cells are generally less efficient in repair between fractions. He may destroy one or more lesion per fraction and does not exceed more than five fractions in a single course. Use this code to report the provider’s professional contribution to the patient management during the course of stereotactic body radiotherapy treatment. The provider performs the patient’s examination for medical evaluation and management that includes assessment of the patient’s response to treatment, coordination of care and treatment, and review of imaging and/or lab test results. He also reviews port films, dosimetry, dose delivery, and other treatment parameters. He also evaluates the treatment set up and the use of blocks and wedges. short_description: Intraoperative radiation treatment management
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider manages the complete course of intraoperative radiation treatment in which he administers radiation therapy in the form of irradiating X–rays or electron beams directly to the exposed tumor during surgery. Explanation Radiation oncology, also called radiotherapy, applies high–frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. For this code, the provider performs management for the treatment of cancers that are difficult to remove completely during surgery. The goal of the treatment is to deliver the high dose of radiation precisely to the target area with minimal exposure of surrounding normal tissue. Providers may perform intraoperative radiation treatment with electron beams and X–rays. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs special radiotherapy procedures requiring special consideration from the provider in the overall management of radiotherapy treatment. The goal is to kill the cancer cells throughout the body or to destroy the immune system so that it will not reject a transplanted organ. short_description: Proton treatment delivery; simple, without compensation
lay_term: This code represents the technical component of a procedure in which the provider administers radiation therapy using a beam of protons to irradiate the cancer. The treatment performed is simple, using a single non–tangential port and without compensators. Explanation Proton therapy involves irradiating the cancer cells with a proton beam. This code represents treatment delivery, which is the technical component of a procedure in which the provider performs simple treatment using a single non–tangential port without any compensator. A proton is a positively charged particle that is a part of an atom. These protons interfere with the DNA of tumor cells and minimize their ability to multiply. Proton therapy is more advantageous than standard X–ray radiation because protons enter the body with a low dose of radiation, which increases when the beam slows down within the target tumor, and then the proton stops. A proton beam has a low entrance dose, a high dose designed to cover the entire tumor, and no exit dose beyond the tumor. That is why proton therapy is used to treat deep–seated tumors that are close to sensitive structures like the spinal cord and brain. Terminology Compensator: A solid device that shapes the radiation beam passing through it in a way that it provides the maximum dose to the tumor and minimizes the exposure of healthy tissues. Port: A point of entry of treatment. Radiation oncology: Radiation oncology, also called radiotherapy, applies high–frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. Tips Use 77522 for delivery of simple proton therapy with compensation. Read Less

short_description: Hyperthermia, externally generated; deep (ie, heating to depths greater than 4 cm) Notes: (For intraoperative hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy [HIPEC], see 96547, 96548)
lay_term: The provider exposes tissue deeper than 4cm in a body site to high temperatures, of up to 113 degrees Fahrenheit, in a technique known as hyperthermia. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and positioned, the provider positions external applicators around the body cavity or organ to be treated, directing the energy at the target area or tumor. She also attaches temperature sensors to the skin above or near the tumor or inserts probes to measure the temperature of the target area or tumor to ensure the desired temperature is reached, but not exceeded. She determines the type and number of applicators and temperature sensors to apply based upon the size and location of the tumor. As she begins the warming process, she administers a moderate anesthesia to ease discomfort. She completes the heat distribution phase and continues to monitor the patient for two hours or more. She performs the hyperthermia along with radiation or chemotherapy treatments. Terminology Hyperthermia: Therapeutic technique that exposes body tissue to high, sustained temperatures, up to 113 degrees Fahrenheit, to treat cancer; the heat is generated by a variety of heat delivery systems or probes such as radiofrequency electrodes, microwave antennae, ultrasound transducers, and hot source methods like hot water, ferromagnetic seeds, nanoparticles, and resistive implants; providers perform it in conjunction with radiation or chemotherapies to improve the effect of these treatments; also known as thermal therapy or thermotherapy. Tips The consistent, sustained, high temperatures of this therapy, increases cell metabolism, which helps to shrink tumors by damaging or killing the cancer cells. The heat also improves the effects of radiation or chemotherapy when combined with these treatments. Providers primarily use this type of heat treatment to treat cancers within the body, such as cervical or bladder cancer. short_description: Hyperthermia generated by interstitial probe(s); 5 or fewer interstitial applicators

Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts one to five probes or needles into the tumor. short_description: Thyroid uptake, single or multiple quantitative measurement(s) (including stimulation, suppression, or discharge, when performed)
lay_term: The provider examines the thyroid gland at selected times following oral administration of radioiodine to determine the amount that reaches the thyroid within a 4 to 24 hour period after ingestion. These measurements identify whether the gland is overactive, underactive, or functioning normally. Providers generally run this study to determine the reasons for thyrotoxicosis, which is an excess of thyroid hormone in the body, which may be caused by Graves' disease, an autoimmune hyperthyroidism, or overactive thyroid. Explanation In this study, the provider administers a small oral dose of radioiodine either in pill form or liquid. He advises the patient to return once or twice within 4 to 24 hours after ingesting the radioactive iodine. At each of the arranged return visits, the provider uses a non–imaging gamma probe or scintillation detector and places it over the front of the patient’s neck, so the entire thyroid gland is detected. He measures the amount of radioiodine absorbed by the thyroid. He has the patient return a second time for a follow–up test to obtain a second set of uptake readings. The provider then compares them with the first set to determine how much hormone has been formed and secreted. Prior to or during the examinations, he may administer medication to stimulate, suppress, or affect discharge of the radioiodine from the thyroid. He then compares the findings and any additional relevant prior studies. He calculates the percentages of radioiodine uptake; interprets the results; and dictates, reviews, and signs the nuclear medicine report. Terminology Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Uptake: Absorption of a substance like iodine or a radiopharmaceutical by a tissue or organ. Tips Report 78012 only once, even for multiple measurements. short_description: Thyroid imaging (including vascular flow, when performed)

short_description: Parathyroid planar imaging (including subtraction, when performed)
lay_term: The provider performs a study to image the parathyroid glands, taking two sets of images after administering very small amounts of two different radiopharmaceuticals or radioactive tracers. The provider takes the results and normalizes or compares them to each other and in some cases performs a subtraction study, to help identify abnormal tissue. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and positioned, the provider verifies the positioning and may give the patient a sedative to ensure the patient remains still through the entire study. She then administers the first radioactive tracers and takes early and delayed planar images of the neck and mediastinum with a Gamma camera. She follows up with a subsequent tracer and repeats the images. She may take additional images of the neck during each tracer administration as needed. She digitally stores the studies acquired, then manipulates and compares the images with other clinical data. The provider may also perform the test subsequent to an administration of iodine–containing preparations, which aid in the comparison of the images during a subtraction study. If she performs a subtraction study, she compares the two sets of images to help her distinguish abnormal parathyroid tissue from normal parathyroid tissue. For example, abnormal tissue will appear to her as an area of increased uptake of certain radiopharmaceuticals on the initial images. The subsequent delayed images will show an even more pronounced absorption. The provider reviews the findings with the ordering physician and dictates, then reviews and signs the nuclear medicine report. The provider performs this study to identify benign tumors, such as parathyroid adenomas, malignant parathyroid carcinoma, or hyperplastic parathyroid glands, which is an enlargement of all four of the parathyroid glands. Terminology Gamma camera: Device that detects the pattern of distribution of radioactive material in the body and sends this information to a computer; also called a scintillation camera or Anger camera, named after its inventor Hal Anger. Mediastinum: The space between the lungs, containing the heart and its large vessels, trachea, esophagus, thymus, lymph nodes, and other structures and tissues. Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical also called radiotracers or tracers, emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Parathyroid glands: Glands located beneath the thyroid gland in the neck that secrete hormones, called parathormone or parathyrin, which regulate calcium and phosphorus metabolism by the body. Planar imaging: Nuclear medicine study that produces a two–dimensional image of a three–dimensional object by taking two sets of pictures and using dual radiotracers. Uptake: Absorption of a substance like iodine or a radiopharmaceutical by a tissue or organ. Tips If you only do planar dual phase imaging of the neck and mediastinum, use 78070. If you do SPECT dual phase imaging of the neck and mediastinum, with limited planar imaging, report 78071. Do not bill for two or more units as multiple imaging is common and inherent in the resources required for 78070. If you are reporting only the physician’s interpretation for the radiology service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the radiology code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the radiology service, you would append modifier TC to the radiology code. Note, however, that payer policy may exempt hospitals from appending modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the radiology code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Read Less

short_description: Adrenal imaging, cortex and/or medulla
lay_term: The provider performs a functional imaging technique for evaluation and identification of abnormal adrenal function. After administering an intravenous injection of a radiolabeled cholesterol or radioactive tracer, the provider schedules the patient to return for imaging within three to seven days depending upon the clinical reason for the study. The provider also orders other medications for the patient to take in a prescribed dose and time before returning for imaging. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and positioned, the provider administers a slow intravenous injection of an adrenal tracer or radiolabeled cholesterol, such as NB–59. He orders medications such as potassium iodide to block absorption of the tracer by the thyroid and a laxative to reduce radioactivity in the colon by helping with excretion of the radioactive tracer. He then schedules the patient to return for serial imaging within a two to seven–day period, with the timing of imaging sequences determined by the clinical reason for testing. The provider takes planar images with a Gamma camera, and the images are stored in the computer. He may take additional images as needed to help with localization of a tumor. He compares the images, evaluating the uptake of tracer material in the adrenal glands, and analyzes and interprets them. The provider reviews the findings with the ordering physician and dictates, reviews, and signs the nuclear medicine report. This study detects benign tumors, such as adrenal adenomas, and malignant tumors, such as adrenal carcinomas, and can differentiate between cortical and medullary tumors or determine causes of Cushing's syndrome. Terminology Adrenal: Refers to the adrenal glands, located at the top of each kidney, or their secretions. Cortex: Outer layer of an organ or body structure, as of the kidney or adrenal gland. Cushing’s syndrome: A hormonal disorder of the body caused by prolonged exposure to high levels of the hormone cortisol. Gamma camera: Device that detects the pattern of distribution of radioactive material in the body and sends this information to a computer; also called a scintillation camera or Anger camera, named after its inventor Hal Anger. Medulla: Innermost part of an organ. short_description: Bone marrow imaging; multiple areas
lay_term: The provider images the bone tissue after intravenous administration of a radiopharmaceutical, or radiotracer, distributes and collects in the body. This noninvasive study images multiple body sites and may be done in multiple phases. Explanation In this study, the provider intravenously injects a radiopharmaceutical or tracer, such as Tc–99m sulfur colloid. The tracer is carried by the patient’s blood stream and absorbed by the bones. Depending upon the reason for the study, the provider may take images immediately, after a delay, or in phases after a two to four hour wait to allow for bone absorption. If she is imaging the pelvic bone, she may ask the patient to void to ensure the urinary bladder is not concentrated with material, which may obscure part of the pelvic bone. She positions a gamma camera against the body part to be examined and records the images of the tracer distribution in the bone. She moves the camera and/or table during the study to capture the images. She analyzes the images to assess for disease. She looks for evidence of abnormal bone metabolism that shows up as darker hot spots and brighter cold spots where the tracers have or haven't accumulated. The provider reviews the findings with the referring physician and dictates, reviews, and signs the nuclear medicine report. This imaging evaluates the activity of bone marrow in multiple diseases such as metastatic disease, a cancer that has spread or metastasized from one area of the body to another, or to diagnose leukemia, unexplained bone pain, osteomyelitis, or bone infection. The test may also help to determine the best location for bone marrow biopsy. Terminology Bone marrow: Soft tissue found at the core of some bones that manufacture blood cells. Gamma camera: Device that detects the pattern of distribution of radioactive material in the body and sends this information to a computer; also called a scintillation camera or Anger camera, named after its inventor. Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Tips Providers often use this study to evaluate suspected diseases of the hips, lower back, or jaw. Imaging usually takes an additional 30–45 minutes as the camera circles completely around the target area or the provider uses multiple cameras to create a cross–sectional image. This helps pinpoint the location of the abnormality being evaluated. short_description: Bone marrow imaging; whole body
lay_term: The provider scans the entire body after intravenous administration of a radiopharmaceutical, or radiotracer, into the body. This noninvasive study images the entire skeleton in intervals to capture the tracer’s movement through the body. Explanation In this study, the provider administers a radiopharmaceutical or radiotracer such as Tc–99m sulfur colloid. short_description: Plasma volume, radiopharmaceutical volume-dilution technique (separate procedure); single sampling
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider determines the plasma volume, a blood component, by introducing a known quantity of radioactive material into the blood and measuring the concentration after adequate mixing. This code represents a single sample method. Explanation Radiopharmaceutical volume–dilution technique uses a radiopharmaceutical substance as a radioactive tracer for quantification of blood components like plasma volume, red blood cell volume, white blood cell volume, etc. In this procedure the provider determines the plasma volume by introducing a radioactive tracer like iodinated albumin by injection. He injects the iodinated albumin directly into a vein and then after a specified time, such as 20 minutes, he withdraws a blood sample using an appropriate anticoagulant. From the concentration of the tracer in the sample the provider can calculate the volume in which the tracer is distributed. He then calculates the plasma volume by centrifuging a part of the blood sample and measuring radioactivity of an exact volume of plasma using a mathematical formula. Use this code when the provider takes a single blood sample to determine the plasma volume and does not perform the test as part of a larger procedure. Terminology Anticoagulant: A drug that prevents the clotting of the blood. Centrifuging: A process in which a centrifuge is used to separate liquids of different densities. Radiopharmaceutical: A combination of a radioactive compound with a pharmaceutical compound. Tips Use 78111 when the provider takes multiple blood samples to determine the plasma volume. The entity that bears the cost of the radiopharmaceutical may report the radiopharmaceutical substance separately using the appropriate code. short_description: Red cell volume determination (separate procedure); single sampling
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider determines the red cell volume, a blood component, by introducing a known quantity of red blood cells tagged with a radioactive tracer and measuring the concentration after adequate mixing. This code represents a single sample method. Explanation In this procedure, the provider begins by removing a sample of patient blood. In a typical test, she keeps a portion of the sample to prepare as a standard, and in another portion, she tags the red blood cells with a radiopharmaceutical such as Cr–51 sodium chromate. She prepares the standard sample by diluting a known volume of red blood cells with a known volume of water. She then injects into a vein the sample that contains red blood cells tagged with a radioactive tracer. After a gap of time, such as 15 minutes, she withdraws a blood sample. She uses the sample to determine the red cell volume by comparing it with the standard and by using a mathematical formula. Use this code when the provider takes a single blood sample to determine the red blood cell volume and does not perform the test as part of a larger service. Providers most commonly perform this test on patients with elevated hematocrit levels to determine if the problem is due to increased red blood cells or simply decreased plasma volume. Terminology Hematocrit level: Percentage of the volume of a blood sample made of red blood cells. Radiopharmaceutical: A combination of a radioactive compound with a pharmaceutical compound. Tips Use 78121 when the provider takes multiple blood samples to determine the plasma volume. short_description: Red cell volume determination (separate procedure); multiple samplings
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider determines the red cell volume, a blood component, by introducing a known quantity of red blood cells tagged with a radioactive tracer and measuring the concentration after adequate mixing. This code represents a multiple sample method. Explanation In this procedure, the provider begins by removing a sample of patient blood. In a typical test, he keeps a portion of the sample to prepare as a standard, and in another portion, he tags the red blood cells with a radiopharmaceutical such as Cr–51 sodium chromate. He prepares the standard sample by diluting a known volume of red blood cells with a known volume of water. He then injects into a vein the sample that contains red blood cells tagged with a radioactive tracer. He then withdraws three blood samples at different time intervals, such as 15, 20, and 25 minutes. He uses the samples to determine the red cell volume by comparing them with the standard and by using a mathematical formula. Use this code when the provider takes multiple blood samples to determine the red blood cell volume and does not perform the test as part of a larger service. Providers most commonly perform this test on patients with elevated hematocrit levels to determine if the problem is due to increased red blood cells or simply decreased plasma volume. Terminology Hematocrit levels: Percentage of the volume of blood sample made of red blood cells. Radiopharmaceutical: A combination of a radioactive compound with a pharmaceutical compound. Tips Use 78120 when the provider takes a single blood sample to determine the plasma volume. The entity that bears the cost of the radiopharmaceutical may report the radiopharmaceutical substance separately using the appropriate code. If you are reporting only the professional component for the radiology service, you should append modifier 26, professional component, to the radiology code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the radiology service, you would append modifier TC to the radiology code.
