short_description: Whole blood volume determination, including separate measurement of plasma volume and red cell volume (radiopharmaceutical volume-dilution technique)
lay_term: The provider performs a study to measure the patient’s whole blood volume, including red blood cell and plasma volumes. The test involves injecting the patient with a radiopharmaceutical or radiotracer and his own red blood cells that have been tagged with a tracer. The provider then calculates the volumes using an isotope dilution principle. It determines the volume of these items by introducing a known quantity of radiopharmaceuticals into an unknown volume of blood and measuring the concentration after adequate mixing. Explanation In this study, the provider begins by removing a sample of patient blood. In a typical test, she keeps a portion for a patient blank, keeps another portion to prepare the standard, and in another portion she tags the red blood cells with a radiopharmaceutical such as Cr–51 sodium chromate. She prepares two identical doses of the chromium labeled red blood cells from the tagged portion. She uses one dose to prepare the standard and the other to re–infuse the patient. She also prepares two doses of I–125 labeled human serum albumin, a protein tracer. Again, she uses one to prepare a standard and the other to inject into the patient. She injects the patient with both radiopharmaceuticals through the same intravenous line, administering the labeled red cells first and the albumin second. After waiting for the labeled blood to circulate, she collects three samples in 10–minute intervals. She determines the hematocrit of the samples. She compares the radioactivity of equal portions of the patient’s whole blood, the standard vials, and the patient blank in a scintillation counter. The provider then calculates the total blood, red cell, and plasma volumes, reviews the findings with the referring physician, and dictates, reviews, and signs the nuclear medicine report. This study helps diagnose the reasons for an increase in red blood cell mass and total blood volume, for a white blood cell count above the normal range, and when the body produces too many blood platelets. Terminology Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Radiopharmaceutical volume–dilution technique: A blood volume analysis technique that mixes a tracer substance, such as albumin I–131, into an unknown volume, then places an identical amount of tracer into a known volume; by comparing the concentration of the tracer between the known and unknown volumes, the provider obtains an exact measurement of the unknown volume. short_description: Red cell survival study
lay_term: The provider studies the lifespan of a red blood cell after injecting the patient with the patient's own red blood cells that have been tagged with a radiopharmaceutical. Explanation In this study, the provider first measures the patient’s red blood cell volume. He then withdraws a sample of blood, separates the red blood cells, and tags them with a radiopharmaceutical such as chromium CR–51. He re–injects them into the patient and takes an initial blood sample. He repeats the blood sampling over the next few weeks or until the volume of the tagged red blood cells drops to half of the initial blood sample. He also draws whole blood samples at each visit and records the hematocrit levels or the percentage of the volume of whole blood that is made up of red blood cells. He takes all the samples collected for the red blood cell survival study, centrifuges them, and obtains counts on a gamma or scintillation counter that is attached to a computer. He then calculates red blood cell counts and extrapolates the data to determine the patient’s red blood cell survival as compared to the norm. The provider interprets the results, then dictates, reviews, and signs the nuclear medicine report. The exam determines the cause of anemia of unknown etiology when a provider suspects that the bone marrow is unable to replace the red blood cells that are being prematurely destroyed, either due to a genetic defect, infection, or the patient’s own antibodies attacking the red blood cells and causing them to break down too early. Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Scintillation counter: An instrument that detects and counts the flashes of light or scintillations produced by a radiopharmaceutical. short_description: Labeled red cell sequestration, differential organ/tissue (eg, splenic and/or hepatic)
lay_term: The provider studies the liver and spleen after injecting the patient with the patient's own red blood cells that have been tagged with a radiopharmaceutical. Explanation In this study, the provider withdraws a sample of blood, separates the red blood cells, and tags them with a radiopharmaceutical such as chromium CR–51. She retains a portion of the tagged red blood cells as a standard measure and re–injects another equal portion into the patient. After the injection of the tagged red blood cells, she marks the location of the heart, spleen, and liver on the patient’s skin to take measurements at the exact same location each time she scans the patient. She waits 24 hours, then uses a probe or scintillation counter, which is an instrument that detects and counts the flashes of light or scintillations produced by the chromium. She places the probe directly on the skin of the pre–marked areas, records the counts, and compares various ratios. The provider interprets the results, then dictates, reviews, and signs the nuclear medicine report. The exam determines if the liver or spleen is the site of premature destruction of red cells. Terminology Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Splenic sequestration study: Nuclear medicine study that determines if the liver or spleen is the site of the premature destruction of red cells. short_description: Spleen imaging only, with or without vascular flow Notes: (If combined with liver study, use procedures 78215 and 78216)
lay_term: The provider studies the spleen after intravenous administration of a radiopharmaceutical, or radiotracer, to determine the size and position of the spleen or to detect tumors, abscesses, or cysts. Explanation In this study, the provider intravenously administers a radiopharmaceutical or radiotracer such as technetium 99 sulfur colloid. If he is doing a vascular flow study, he positions the patient under the camera before administering the radiotracer. In this way, he has the blood flow information on any defect that he finds. He allows sufficient time, usually 10 to 20 minutes, then takes planar images of the spleen using a gamma camera. To help in determination of the spleen size, he places a reference marker on the left costal margin, meaning the lower edge of the thorax or chest formed by the bottom edge of the ribcage, before taking an image. When he finishes the study, the provider interprets the results, then dictates, reviews, and signs the nuclear medicine report. Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Planar imaging: Nuclear medicine study that produces a two–dimensional image of a three–dimensional object. Reference marker: An object placed in the field of view of an imaging system, which appears in the image for the provider to use as a point of reference or a measure. short_description: Platelet survival study
lay_term: The provider studies platelet lifespan after drawing a sample of the patient’s blood, tagging the platelets with a radiopharmaceutical, and then re–transfusing them into the patient. Explanation In this study, the provider draws a sample of blood and tags the patient’s platelets with a radiopharmaceutical such as Indium In 111 oxyquinoline, then re–transfuses them into the patient. She then collects blood samples, determining the number and timing of the samples based upon the purpose of the study and the average time she expects the platelets to survive. At a minimum though she takes blood samples at 20 minutes, 2 hours, 3 hours, and 4 hours after injecting the tagged platelets, and then daily for up to 10 days or until in general the level of radioactivity reduces to 10 percent of the maximum activity. If she expects platelet survival will be short, she takes additional samples on the first day. The provider interprets the results, then dictates, reviews, and signs the nuclear medicine report. The study helps diagnose and monitor diseases such as thrombocytopenia, a deficiency of platelets in the blood that can be caused by excessive destruction or pooling of platelets as a result of the patient’s own antibodies attacking the platelets; aplastic anemia, when the body stops producing enough new blood cells; leukemia, a cancer of the blood or bone marrow causing an abnormal increase of immature white blood cells or blasts; and other diseases. Terminology Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Platelets: Element found in blood plasma that promotes blood clotting. short_description: Lymphatics and lymph nodes imaging Notes: (For sentinel node identification without scintigraphy imaging, use 38792) (For sentinel node excision, see 38500-38542)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses a gamma–emitting radioactive tracer to diagnose and localize diseases of the lymphatics and lymph nodes. Explanation Nuclear diagnostic imaging is an imaging technique that uses a radioactive substance or tracer to diagnose and treat disease. The goal of this procedure is to identify the sentinel lymph node and to identify the points of blockage in the lymphatic system. A sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node in the body that tumor cells reach from the primary tumor. Depending upon the area of the body where the lymph nodes are to be examined, the provider injects the radioactive tracer into the skin or other tissue surrounding the site of the tumor. The tracer gives off energy in the form of gamma rays, which the provider scans using an external gamma camera. A computer uses this data to make images of the area. Usually the provider takes images after a time gap of 1–2 hours. This entire process is also called lymphoscintigraphy. Terminology Lymphatics: Network of small channels similar to blood vessels that circulate the fluid called lymph. Lymph glands: Small oval shaped glands that are made up of lymphatic tissue and that filter the lymph. Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Radioactive tracer: A chemical substance that providers use to track the distribution of a substance within a natural system such as a cell or tissue. Tips Use 38792 when the provider performs radioactive tracer injection to identify a sentinel node without imaging. Do not report 38792 in addition to 78195 when the provider injects the radiopharmaceutical and performs lymph node imaging at the same session. short_description: Liver imaging; static only
lay_term: A liver and spleen scan is a specialized radiologic procedure that is used to examine the liver and spleen to identify certain conditions or to assess their function. Explanation The patient is placed on the table in the supine position. After cleaning the site on arm with antiseptic solution, a small amount of the radioactive tracer is injected. After approximately 30 minutes, the scanner is placed over the right upper quadrant of the abdomen in order to detect the gamma rays emitted by the radionuclide in the liver and spleen tissue. Tips For nuclear medicine, use CPT® code 78201 (Liver imaging; static only) includes the term "static only" to differentiate it from 78202 (… with vascular flow). The service that CPT® code 78201 describes involves a special camera taking planar images of the liver by detecting gamma radiation from a radioisotope injected into a peripheral vein and extracted by the liver. Use CPT® code 78202 for a procedure that also requires imaging by detecting the radioisotope radiation but adds imaging of blood flow by labeling red blood cells. Read Less

short_description: Hepatobiliary system imaging, including gallbladder when present
lay_term: The provider images the liver, bile, bile ducts, and gallbladder to follow the production and flow of bile from the liver to the small intestine to diagnose a bile duct obstruction or leakage; abnormalities in the bile ducts; gallbladder inflammation known as cholecystitis; gallstones; or other disorders that affect the hepatobiliary system. This exam is also known as hepatobiliary scintigraphy. Explanation In this study, the provider injects the patient with a radiopharmaceutical or iminodiacetic acid tracer such as 99mTc–disofenin or 99mTc–mebrofenin. She uses a gamma camera to obtain the images of the abdomen and trace the substance as it travels through the bloodstream to the liver, where it's absorbed by the bile, then moves with the bile to the gallbladder, bile ducts, and to the small intestine. The provider takes pictures continuously for about an hour, monitoring the scan's progress on a monitor. If she does not see the gallbladder within the hour, she will take delayed images for up to 3 to 4 hours. In some cases, she may need delayed imaging at 18 to 24 hours. She stops the scan when the tracer enters the small intestine. Terminology Gamma camera: Device that detects the pattern of distribution of radioactive material in the body and sends this information to a computer; also called a scintillation camera or Anger camera, named after its inventor. Hepatobiliary: Relating to the liver, bile, bile ducts, and gallbladder. Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Tips Use 78226 to report studies where the provider performs imaging alone. Use 78227 when the provider performs imaging in conjunction with an assessment of the gallbladder and hepatic function by pharmacologic intervention. Both 78226 and78227 measure gallbladder ejection fraction and you may see either commonly referred to as a HIDA scan. short_description: Esophageal motility
lay_term: The provider images the esophagus to test muscle movement or contractions and esophagus peristalsis. The patient swallows a radiopharmaceutical or tracer in water, and the provider takes a rapid sequence of images. The study is also known as esophageal transit scintigraphy. Explanation In this study, the provider gives the patient a radiopharmaceutical or tracer such as 99mTc sulfur colloid in water, and the provider has the patient swallow the liquid. Depending upon the focus of the study, the patient consumes the liquid in one swallow or in six single swallows, at intervals of 15 or 30 seconds between each. As the patient swallows, the provider takes planar images of the swallowing process from the oral cavity down to the stomach by using a gamma camera that tracks the tracer as it travels down the esophagus. The provider determines how long the swallowing takes, including a calculation of transit time and any liquid retained in the mouth, throat, or esophagus. He may take a static image at the end of the exam to evaluate the presence of any tracheobronchial aspirate. He also repeats the exam as needed after an interval of 30 minutes, this time with a gelatinous semi–liquid tracer. short_description: Gastric mucosa imaging
lay_term: The provider images the lining of the stomach, called the gastric mucosa, after intravenous administration of a radiopharmaceutical or tracer. short_description: Gastroesophageal reflux study

short_description: Gastrointestinal protein loss
lay_term: The provider analyzes the stool after intravenous injection of a patient with a radiopharmaceutical or tracer. The analysis detects and quantifies an abnormal loss of protein from the digestive tract or the inability of the digestive tract to absorb proteins. This occurs from conditions such as bacteria or parasite infection of the intestines, Crohn’s disease, lymphoma, or other diseases. Explanation In this study, the provider intravenously injects a radiopharmaceutical or tracer such as 51CR chromic chloride. He draws an equal amount of the chromic chloride and adds it to a gallon container, filling it with water. He then instructs the patient to begin collecting all fecal samples in containers with lids beginning the next morning and for the next 5–day period and then deliver them to the provider for testing. When the patient returns the specimens, the provider adds an enzyme and water to each container and mixes well. After waiting 24–hours he draws a sample from each of the containers, including the standard, and compares the amount of tracer in each bucket to the standard. He calculates the total percent dose of the tracer excreted to quantify the protein loss. He then interprets the results, and dictates, reviews, and signs the nuclear medicine report. short_description: Intestine imaging (eg, ectopic gastric mucosa, Meckel's localization, volvulus)
lay_term: Intestinal imaging for diagnosis of ectopic gastric mucosa leads to localization of Meckel's diverticulum, an appendage in the ileocecal region. It is the residue of the omphalomesenteric duct (yolk stalk) that normally should disappear during the fetal development. The radionuclear imaging procedure, also known as Meckel's scan or scintigraphy, uses a larger field–of–view (LFOV) gamma camera to detect the concentration of radioactive substances (radioisotopes such as technetium–99m pertechnetate, injected intravenously) in ectopic gastric mucosa in the diverticulum. The patient is asked to stop food intake at least four hours prior to the procedure. The imaging takes about 30 minutes to complete, excluding the pre–imaging procedures and formalities. Explanation The patient is administered pharmacological agents such as cimetidine or ranitidine prior to the imaging process. These agents help in accumulation of radioactive substance in the ectopic gastric mucosa for better imaging. After allowing sufficient time for these substances to start their effect (at least one hour), the patient is injected with a predetermined dose of Tc–99m pertechnetate (a radioisotope) intravenously and put in a supine position. The gamma camera is put above the right lower quadrant region of the abdomen. The camera acquires two sets of sequential images (1–2 seconds/frame for 60 seconds of anterior flow followed by 15–30 seconds/frame for 29 minutes in the dynamic acquisition mode) that is processed and stored by the computer. Static films may be acquired at the rate of 2–5 seconds/frame of the anterior flow and 300–500k static images of the anterior at 5 minutes interval for 30 minutes if computer acquisition of dynamic images is not possible. The Tc–99m injected prior to the filming highlights the regions of ectopic gastric mucosa, intestinal obstruction or diverticulum and is captured by the high–resolution gamma camera. Once the imaging procedure is over, the patient may be given an oral dose of potassium perchlorate to neutralize the effect of Tc–99m pertechnetate concentration in the thyroid gland. Terminology Ectopic gastric mucosa: Gastric mucosa is a layer of mucous membrane that covers the internal walls of the stomach. Ectopic gastric mucosa refers to the presence of gastric mucosal tissue outside the stomach. Meckel's diverticulum is one place where the gastric mucosa is found in high concentration and radionuclear imaging techniques use radioactive substances that highlight the presence of the ectopic gastric mucosa in the diverticulum, indicating its presence and location. Meckel's diverticulum: Meckel's diverticulum is a congenital abnormality of the digestive system that forms in the early stage of fetal development as a small pouch at the junction of the two intestines near the cecum. It is the residue of the omphalomesenteric duct (yolk stalk) which connects the terminal ileum to the umbilicus and yolk sac and normally should disappear by the seventh week of fetal development but fails to do so completely, resulting in Meckel's diverticulum. It is named after the German anatomist Johann F. Meckel. The diverticulum can result in complications such as diverticulitis, intestinal hemorrhage, tumor, and intestinal obstruction, mostly accompanied by acute abdominal pain. CT scans or radionuclide scans are used for definitive diagnosis and surgical excision of the diverticulum is the only treatment option. Volvulus: It refers to an abnormal twist in the intestine that results in intestinal obstruction. This causes vomiting, severe pain, and abdominal distention. It can lead to hampered blood supply (ischemia) to the obstructed part of the intestine and, ultimately, necrosis. In nuclear medicine imaging, radiopharmaceuticals are taken internally –– for example, intravenously or orally. Then, external detectors (gamma cameras) capture and form images from the radiation emitted by the radiopharmaceuticals. This process is unlike a diagnostic X–ray where external radiation is passed through the body to form an image. Tips This service is a type of nuclear medicine imaging procedure. Supply of radiopharmaceuticals used in the imaging process can be coded separately using HCPCS codes. Read Less

short_description: Peritoneal-venous shunt patency test (eg, for LeVeen, Denver shunt) Notes: (For injection procedure, use 49427)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider evaluates the peritoneal–venous shunt to ensure that it is not blocked and is functioning well. He then evaluates the resulting images to check the tracer distribution throughout the peritoneal cavity. short_description: Bone density (bone mineral content) study, 1 or more sites; single photon absorptiometry
lay_term: The provider uses a single energy photon beam to measure the bone mineral density, or BMD, which is the amount of minerals per unit area in the bone or bones. The goal of the procedure is to measure the mineral content of the bones to rule out diseases, such as osteoporosis. This code represents both the technical and professional components of the service. Explanation Single photon absorptiometry applies a single beam of ionizing radiation with a particular energy to measure the amount of mineral mass in the bone or bones as the beam passes through them. This code represents the technical and professional components of a service in which the provider passes a single photon beam through the bone and soft tissue at one or more sites in the appendicular, or peripheral, skeleton. He allows this beam to fall on the detector and determines the amount of mineral in the bone. He often uses the distal radius as the site of measurement to determine age related diseases such as osteoporosis as there is a smaller amount of soft tissue in this area. Terminology Bone mineral density, BMD: Measurement of the amount of minerals in the bones, which in turn reflects their strength. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Dual photon absorptiometry: Measurement of bone mineral density with the help of photons of two different energy levels. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Peripheral: Along the outside boundary or edges. Photon: A particle of light that carries energy equivalent to the radiation frequency. Osteoporosis: Medical conditions in which the bones become weak because of loss of calcium, making the patient prone to fractures. Radius: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the lateral, or outside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the thumb. Single photon absorptiometry: Measurement of bone mineral density with the help of photons of single energy. short_description: Myocardial imaging, positron emission tomography (PET), metabolic evaluation study (including ventricular wall motion[s] and/or ejection fraction[s], when performed), single study
lay_term: In this diagnostic procedure, the provider performs positron emission tomography, a type of nuclear imaging test, of the heart to evaluate heart metabolism, such as oxygen, glucose, or drug metabolism. The service also includes ventricular wall motion orejection fraction or both, if performed. This code is for a single study. Explanation Myocardial imaging by positron emission tomography (PET) scan is a diagnostic nuclear medicine imaging procedure that produces three–dimensional images to show how the heart muscle is working. The provider injects a radioactive tracer or radionuclide into the bloodstream of the patient. This radionuclide is created by applying a radioactive atom to any biological compound or drug. The radionuclide travels in the bloodstream to the heart and breaks in the target area into tiny positively charged particles called positrons, which emit gamma rays. The provider uses a special device called a PET scanner that detects the gamma rays given off by the radioactive substance. The computer then processes the emitted data to produce multidimensional images of the distribution of the drug or biological compound throughout the heart muscle. The provider may also evaluate ventricular wall motion (the pumping action of the heart) and the ejection fraction (the percentage of blood pumped out of a filled ventricle with each heartbeat). These images help the provider in metabolic evaluation. He can draw inferences about whether the heart muscle is functioning normally or not. After evaluating the heart function, the provider prepares a report. Terminology Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. short_description: Myocardial imaging, positron emission tomography (PET), metabolic evaluation study (including ventricular wall motion[s] and/or ejection fraction[s], when performed), single study; with concurrently acquired computed tomography transmission scan Notes: (For CT coronary calcium scoring, use 75571) (CT performed for other than attenuation correction and anatomical localization is reported using the appropriate site specific CT code with modifier 59)
lay_term: The provider performs a PET myocardial imaging scan, a type of nuclear imaging test with CT transmission scan that tells how the myocardium, the heart muscle, is functioning. The test provides information on metabolism, such as oxygen, glucose, or drug metabolism; ejection fraction and ventricular wall motion studies are included if performed. This code is for a single study. Explanation Myocardial imaging by positron emission tomography (PET) scan is diagnostic nuclear medicine imaging that produces three–dimensional images to show how the heart muscle is working. Simultaneous computed tomography (CT) transmission scanning and PET imaging help the provider determine whether activity is physiologic (i.e., a natural function) as opposed to pathologic (indicative of a disease process). It also helps correct for attenuation, spatial registration and alignment, and motion, and allows for precise localization of radionuclide activity. Concurrent imaging also shortens imaging time. The provider injects a radioactive tracer into the bloodstream of the patient. This radionuclide is created by applying a radioactive atom to any biological compound or drug. The radionuclide travels in the bloodstream and reaches the heart. Once in the target area, this radionuclide breaks into tiny positively charged particles called positrons, which emit gamma rays. The PET and CT scanners detect the gamma rays given off by the radioactive substance. The computer then processes the emitted data to produce multidimensional images of the distribution of the drug or biological compound throughout the heart muscle. The provider may also evaluate ventricular wall motion (the pumping action of the heart) and the ejection fraction (the percentage of blood pumped out of a filled ventricle with each heartbeat). The CT and PET data are fused and presented to the interpreter on a monitor as CT data, PET data, and superimposed CT/PET data. These images help the provider evaluate metabolic function of the heart. Using this data, he can draw inferences about whether the heart muscle is functioning normally or not. Terminology Attenuation: The reduction in strength, amplitude, or force of something, such as a sound signal or wavelength of light. Computed tomography (CT): An imaging procedure in which an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer–generated three–dimensional image of the inside of an object from a large series of two–dimensional X–ray images taken around a single axis of rotation; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Myocardial metabolic evaluation: Evaluation of glucose utilization, fatty acid update, oxidation, mitochondrial function, and amino acid effects on the heart using radiolabeled isotopes and nuclear imaging procedures. Myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI): An imaging study of the vessels of the heart at rest or under stress from exercise that utilizes a radioactive substance introduced into the blood stream to highlight specific tissues. Nuclear medicine: Imaging service that involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Perfusion: The flow of blood through the blood vessels; also refers to the process of perfusion, to instill fluids into an organ or tissues. Pharmacological nuclear stress test: A nuclear imaging study (typically PET or CT) used to evaluate blood flow to and from the heart while the patient exercises or after administration of a drug such as Lexiscan® (regadenoson) to stress the heart. Positron emission tomography (PET): A nuclear medicine imaging technique which produces a three–dimensional image of functional processes in the body; the system detects pairs of gamma rays emitted indirectly by a positron–emitting radionuclide (tracer), which is introduced into the body on a biologically active molecule (glucose). Radioactive tracer: A chemical substance (radionuclide) that can be attached to and track the distribution of a different substance within a natural system such as a cell or tissue; 82Rb, 13NH3, and H2 15O are common radiotracers used in myocardial perfusion studies. Radiopharmaceutical: A combination of a radioactive compound with a pharmaceutical compound used to identify and treat certain diseases or analyze the function of a part of human body under investigation. Ventricular: Pertaining to the lower chambers of the heart or to cavities in the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid. short_description: Myocardial imaging, infarct avid, planar; qualitative or quantitative
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs planar nuclear imaging of heart muscle after the injection of a radioactive substance that accumulates in the area of damaged myocardium. The test helps to identify and locate the damage a recent myocardial infarction might have caused. Myocardial infarction, or MI, is the irreversible damage of the myocardium or heart muscle due to ischemia caused by a blood clot. Explanation Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. lay_term: The provider performs positron emission tomography, a type of nuclear imaging test, of the heart that reveals how the blood flows through the heart. Explanation Myocardial imaging by positron emission tomography (PET) scan is a diagnostic nuclear medicine imaging procedure that produces three–dimensional images to show how the heart is working. The provider injects a radioactive tracer or radionuclide into the bloodstream of the patient. This radionuclide is created by applying a radioactive atom to any biological compound or drug. The radionuclide travels in the bloodstream to the heart and breaks in the target area into tiny positively charged particles called positrons, which emit gamma rays. The provider uses a special device called a PET scanner that detects the gamma rays given off by the radioactive substance. The computer then processes the emitted data to produce multidimensional images of the distribution of the drug or biological compound throughout the heart muscle. The provider obtains three–dimensional images of the heart at rest on the monitor that reveal how blood flows through the heart (perfusion). She also induces stress, using a drug or exercise, and obtains more images, which further help the provider evaluate the perfusion of the heart. The provider may also evaluate ventricular wall motion (the pumping action of the heart) and the ejection fraction (the percentage of blood pumped out of a filled ventricle with each heartbeat). Perfusion: The delivery of oxygenated and nutrient–rich blood to the tissues through the blood vessels; also refers to the process of perfusion, to instill fluids into an organ or tissues. short_description: Myocardial imaging, positron emission tomography (PET), perfusion study (including ventricular wall motion[s] and/or ejection fraction[s], when performed); multiple studies at rest and stress (exercise or pharmacologic)
lay_term: In this diagnostic procedure, the provider performs a myocardial perfusion PET imaging study which means it reveals the flow of oxygenated blood to the heart muscles. The service also includes ventricular wall motion and ejection fraction or both, if performed. This code is for multiple studies and is performed at rest and exercise– or drug–induced stress. Explanation A PET scan provides three–dimensional images of the scanned area that makes it easy to detect an area of the heart that has poor blood flow indicating diseased vessels or poorly functioning ventricles. The provider injects the patient with a radiopharmaceutical tracer called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a radioactive substance containing glucose, about one hour before the imaging is scheduled to begin. The radiotracer spreads in the body through the bloodstream and gets absorbed by the cells and starts emitting small amounts of energy (positrons). The positrons collide with electrons resulting in the production of two photons that travel in opposite directions. The photon emission is captured by the PET scanner and processed by a computer to produce three–dimensional images. The provider obtains three–dimensional images of the heart at rest on the monitor that reveal how blood flows through the heart (perfusion). She also induces stress, using a drug or exercise, and obtains more images, which further help the provider evaluate the perfusion of the heart. The provider may also evaluate ventricular wall motion (the pumping action of the heart) and the ejection fraction (the percentage of blood pumped out of a filled ventricle with each heartbeat). Multiple studies are performed. After evaluating the heart function, the provider prepares a report. In coronary artery disease (CAD) or ischemic heart disease (IHD), blood flow to the heart muscles in the diseased region is significantly depleted or completely absent resulting in reduced metabolic activity detected by the PET scan. A PET scan is more effective than a SPECT scan (single–photon emission computed tomography), angiogram, or an EKG stress test in detecting coronary artery disease (CAD). Ischemic heart disease: A heart condition in which blood supply to the heart muscles through the coronary arteries becomes restricted or blocked due to the deposit of plaques inside the arteries (atherosclerosis) resulting in necrosis and possible heart failure. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. lay_term: The provider performs a PET myocardial imaging scan, a type of nuclear imaging test, using two radionuclide tracers. The provider may also evaluate ventricular wall motion (the pumping action of the heart) and the ejection fraction (the percentage of blood pumped out of a filled ventricle with each heartbeat). short_description: Myocardial imaging, positron emission tomography (PET), combined perfusion with metabolic evaluation study (including ventricular wall motion[s] and/or ejection fraction[s], when performed), dual radiotracer (eg, myocardial viability); with concurrently acquired computed tomography transmission scan Notes: (CT performed for other than attenuation correction and anatomical localization is reported using the appropriate site specific CT code with modifier 59)
lay_term: The provider performs a PET myocardial imaging scan, a type of nuclear imaging test, and concurrent CT transmission scan using two radionuclide tracers. The study reveals blood flow to and from the heart (perfusion) as well as information on metabolism, such as oxygen, glucose, or drug metabolism and myocardial (heart muscle) viability. Ejection fraction and ventricular wall motion studies are included if performed. Explanation Myocardial imaging by positron emission tomography (PET) scan is diagnostic nuclear medicine imaging that produces three–dimensional images to show how the heart muscle is working. Simultaneous computed tomography (CT) transmission scanning and PET imaging help the provider determine whether activity is physiologic (i.e., a natural function) as opposed to pathologic (indicative of a disease process). It also helps correct for attenuation, spatial registration and alignment, and motion, and allows for precise localization of radionuclide activity. Concurrent imaging also shortens imaging time. The provider injects two radioactive tracers into the bloodstream of the patient. The tracers travel in the bloodstream and reach the heart. Once in the target area, the tracers break into tiny positively charged particles called positrons, emitting gamma rays. The PET and CT scanners detect the gamma rays given off by the radioactive substance. The computer then processes the emitted data to produce multidimensional images of the distribution of the drug or biological compound throughout the heart muscle. The provider may also evaluate ventricular wall motion (the pumping action of the heart) and the ejection fraction (the percentage of blood pumped out of a filled ventricle with each heartbeat). The CT and PET data are fused and presented to the interpreter on a monitor as CT data, PET data, and superimposed CT/PET data. These images help the provider evaluate perfusion (blood flow) to and from the heart as well as metabolic function. Using this data, he can draw inferences about whether the heart muscle is functioning normally or not. Terminology Attenuation: The reduction in strength, amplitude, or force of something, such as a sound signal or wavelength of light. Computed tomography (CT): An imaging procedure in which an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer–generated three–dimensional image of the inside of an object from a large series of two–dimensional X–ray images taken around a single axis of rotation; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI): An imaging study of the vessels of the heart at rest or under stress from exercise that utilizes a radioactive substance introduced into the blood stream to highlight specific tissues. Nuclear medicine: Imaging service that involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Perfusion: The flow of blood through the blood vessels; also refers to the process of perfusion, to instill fluids into an organ or tissues. Pharmacological nuclear stress test: A nuclear imaging study (typically PET or CT) used to evaluate blood flow to and from the heart while the patient exercises or after administration of a drug such as Lexiscan® (regadenoson) to stress the heart. Positron emission tomography (PET): A nuclear medicine imaging technique which produces a three–dimensional image of functional processes in the body; the system detects pairs of gamma rays emitted indirectly by a positron–emitting radionuclide (tracer), which is introduced into the body on a biologically active molecule (glucose). Radioactive tracer: A chemical substance (radionuclide) that can be attached to and track the distribution of a different substance within a natural system such as a cell or tissue; 82Rb, 13NH3, and H2 15O are common radiotracers used in myocardial perfusion studies. Radiopharmaceutical: A combination of a radioactive compound with a pharmaceutical compound used to identify and treat certain diseases or analyze the function of a part of human body under investigation. Ventricular: Pertaining to the lower chambers of the heart or to cavities in the brain filled with cerebrospinal fluid. lay_term: The provider uses single–photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), a type of nuclear imaging test, to evaluate how well the heart is pumping blood to other parts of the body while the patient is at rest. The provider uses a technique called gated equilibrium technique. Explanation Single–photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is a nuclear imaging test that combines two technologies, computed tomography and a tracer, which is a radioactive material. Cardiac blood pool imaging is also known as radionuclide ventriculography. It is a diagnostic test for evaluating the left ventricular function. The function of the left ventricle is to pump blood and distribute the blood throughout the body. The goal of this test is to evaluate how well the heart is pumping blood to the rest of the body by checking the heart wall motion and ejection fraction. When the patient is appropriately prepped for the test, the provider injects a bolus of radioactive tracer into the vein of the patient. This radioactive tracer travels toward the heart. The radioactive part of the tracer gives off gamma radiations detected by multi–headed gamma cameras that rotate around the patient. SPECT is different from the conventional planar imaging using a gamma camera as SPECT is able to provide 3–dimensional images of the heart by adding together the 2–dimensional cross–sectional images obtained through the camera. In this test, the provider uses the gated equilibrium technique in which the camera takes a series of images triggered by the heart’s electrical signals. These pictures merge together to create a motion picture of the heart. The goal is to evaluate heart functioning during the heart’s motion to ensure that it’s contracting properly. short_description: Pulmonary ventilation imaging (eg, aerosol or gas)
lay_term: In this diagnostic procedure, the provider performs pulmonary ventilation imaging, a nuclear scan test that evaluates the circulation of air within the patient’s lungs. Explanation Pulmonary ventilation imaging is a type of medical imaging test that measures the ventilation, meaning circulation of air, within the lungs. The goal of this test is to identify the areas of the lung that are capable of ventilation, taking in air. He obtains images of the lungs using a gamma camera that can detect the gamma rays emitted by the radioactive tracer gas. These images from the scan show the areas of the lungs that are not receiving enough air. The provider performs this test to evaluate pneumonia, bronchitis, or other infections. short_description: Brain imaging, less than 4 static views; with vascular flow
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs nuclear diagnostic imaging of the brain using a radiopharmaceutical substance to examine the structure and function of the brain. He performs less than four static views, which are two–dimensional views that show one image at a time. He also evaluates the blood flow to the brain. Explanation In this procedure, the provider administers a small amount of a radiopharmaceutical substance. The type of radiopharmaceutical used depends upon the type of tissue being studied. This radiopharmaceutical substance reaches the specific organ or cellular receptors. The pharmaceutical part acts like a chemical that the body normally uses, so body tissue takes up the radiopharmaceutical. In a functioning brain, tumors or other abnormal tissues take up more of the radiopharmaceutical than the rest of the organ or tissue. In a patient who is brain dead, the provider will not see evidence of the tracer in the brain tissue. The radioactive part gives off gamma radiation that a special device, a gamma camera or probe, detects. This device records the gamma rays given off, and the computer uses this data to make images. Negative cerebral flow indicates brain death. short_description: Brain imaging, positron emission tomography (PET); metabolic evaluation
lay_term: In this diagnostic procedure, the provider performs PET, positron emission tomography, a type of nuclear imaging test. It tells how the brain is functioning with information on metabolism, such as oxygen, glucose, or drug metabolism. Explanation Brain imaging by positron emission tomography or PET scan is diagnostic nuclear medicine imaging that produces three–dimensional images to show how the brain and its tissue are working. In this procedure, the provider injects a radioactive tracer or radionuclide into the bloodstream of the patient. This radionuclide breaks in the target area into tiny positively charged particles called positrons, emitting gamma rays. The provider uses a special device called a PET scanner that detects the gamma rays given off by the radioactive substance. The computer then processes the emitted data to produce multi–dimensional images of the distribution of the drug or biological compound throughout the brain. These images help the provider in metabolic evaluation. He can draw inferences regarding the metabolism of the drug or compound as it travels through the brain. Radioactive tracer or radionuclide: A chemical substance providers use to track the distribution of a substance within a natural system such as a cell or tissue. short_description: Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging; limited area (eg, chest, head/neck)
lay_term: In this diagnostic procedure, the provider performs PET, positron emission tomography, on a small, defined area of the body. PET is a type of nuclear imaging test that produces three dimensional images of functional processes in the body and is an effective method of detecting tumor cells in the body. Explanation Positron emission tomography, or PET, scan is diagnostic nuclear imaging that produces three–dimensional images to show how the body organ and its tissues are working. In this procedure, the provider injects a radioactive tracer or radionuclide into the bloodstream of the patient. This radionuclide is created by applying a radioactive atom to glucose, which is rapidly synthesized by the cancer cells. The radionuclide travels in the bloodstream and reaches the tumor area. In the target area of the chest, head, or neck or other area, this radionuclide breaks into tiny positively charged particles called positrons, thereby emitting gamma rays. The provider uses a special device called a PET scanner that detects the gamma rays given off by the radioactive substance. The computer then processes the emitted data to produce multi–dimensional images of the distribution of the chemicals throughout the structure being examined. These images show the concentration of the tracer taken up by cells and help the provider in differentiating the tumor cells from the normal cells of the body. Use this code when the provider performs PET imaging for a limited area like the chest or neck. Terminology Nuclear medicine: Nuclear medicine imaging involves administering radiopharmaceuticals to the patient; the radiopharmaceutical emits radiation that a scanner detects and produces an image that helps the provider to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Radioactive tracer or radionuclide: A chemical substance providers use to track the distribution of a substance within a natural system such as a cell or tissue. short_description: Positron emission tomography (PET) with concurrently acquired computed tomography (CT) for attenuation correction and anatomical localization imaging; skull base to mid-thigh
lay_term: PET and CT scans are both standard imaging tools that allow doctors to evaluate the location and metabolic actions of tumors or cancer inside the body before beginning an active treatment regimen. When alone, each imaging study has their own benefits and limitations but as the results of these two scans are "fused" together, the combined image provides a more complete picture and information on tumor location and metabolism. Explanation Initially, a person is placed in the PET/CT chamber. CT scanners send X–rays through body which are measured by CT detectors and processed via computer algorithms. CT scans give detailed two–dimensional images of the size, shape and location of internal organs or tumors. For PET scans, an injection of glucose infused with radionuclide (radioactive) material is given to the patient. A PET scan measures important body functions, such as blood flow, oxygen use, and sugar metabolism in bodily organs and tissues, to help doctors assess function. Cancer cells consume more sugar than normal cells, and this faster rate of metabolism is accurately detected and transformed into images via the PET scan. Modern PET/CT scanners use both the PET and CT technology together by fusing the data obtained from both, thereby rectifying the limitation of PET. The highly sensitive PET scan detects the abnormal metabolic activity of tumor cells, and CT provides a detailed picture of internal structure of the targeted organ or tumor for the physician. Terminology Positron emission tomography (PET): A nuclear medicine imaging technique which produces a three–dimensional image of functional processes in the body; the system detects pairs of gamma rays emitted indirectly by a positron–emitting radionuclide (tracer), which is introduced into the body on a biologically active molecule (glucose). Computed tomography (CT): An imaging procedure in which an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer–generated three–dimensional image of the inside of an object from a large series of two–dimensional X–ray images taken around a single axis of rotation; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. short_description: Positron emission tomography (PET) with concurrently acquired computed tomography (CT) for attenuation correction and anatomical localization imaging; whole body Notes: (Report 78811-78816 only once per imaging session) (Computed tomography [CT] performed for other than attenuation correction and anatomical localization is reported using the appropriate site specific CT code with modifier 59)
lay_term: The patient is injected with a radiopharmaceutical tracer called FDG (fluoro–deoxyglucose, a radioactive substance containing glucose) about one hour before the imaging is scheduled to begin. The radiotracer spreads in the body via the blood stream and gets absorbed by cells and starts emitting small amounts of energy (positrons). The positrons collide with electrons resulting in the production of photons that travel in opposite directions. The photon emission is captured by the PET scanner and is processed in a computer to give a three–dimensional image of the body tissues being studied. Cancerous cells display a high radiotracer uptake and are highly visible in the scan in comparison to healthy cells. But the PET scan has a limitation in terms of pinpointing the location of a tumor. This shortcoming is overcome by the combination of a PET and CT. The CT scan produces thin cross–sectional slices of internal organs. The images produced by the PET and the CT are combined together to obtain accurate details about the size and location of a tumor. Images can be obtained for the whole body or for any limited area of the body. Explanation The radiologist uses a combination of PET and CT scans to obtain three–dimensional images of the whole body to detect cancerous cells. The patient is injected with a radiopharmaceutical tracer (a radioactive substance injected into the blood stream to highlight specific characteristics of cells) about one hour before the imaging. The images taken with the PET and CT scans are combined to produce images that pinpoint the presence and location of the cancerous tumor. Terminology PET scans are highly effective in detection of cancerous cells in the body. A PET scan provides a three–dimensional image of the body that makes it easy to detect the presence of a malignant tumor. Cancer cells have a higher metabolic rate than the normal body cells and a PET scan takes advantage of this while imaging. Read Less

short_description: Radiopharmaceutical therapy, by interstitial radioactive colloid administration
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider implants a colloidal radioactive substance contained in wires, small tubes, or seeds directly over the tumor area. Explanation Nuclear medicine therapy is a type of therapy that uses radioactive materials, called radiopharmaceuticals, to treat certain conditions like cancer. A colloidal substance consists of particles dispersed throughout another substance. The particles are too small to see individually with an ordinary light microscope but are incapable of passing through a semipermeable membrane. Radioactive colloidal solution consists of liquid containing radioactive isotopes of different elements. In this procedure, the provider uses the radioactive substance contained in wires, small tubes, or seeds and places them over the tumor area using an applicator. The goal is to minimize unwanted side effects and damage to non–involved organs or nearby structures. Terminology Colloid: A substance that consists of particles dispersed throughout another substance; the particles are too small for resolution with an ordinary light microscope but are incapable of passing through a semipermeable membrane. Nuclear medicine therapy: A type of therapy that uses radioactive materials, called radiopharmaceuticals, to treat certain conditions like cancer. Radiopharmaceutical: A combination of a radioactive compound with a pharmaceutical compound. Semipermeable membrane: A membrane that allows only certain molecules to pass through. short_description: Radiopharmaceutical therapy, by intra-articular administration
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider injects a radioactive substance into a joint to alleviate the synovial inflammation. Explanation Nuclear medicine therapy is a type of therapy that uses radioactive materials, called radiopharmaceuticals, to treat certain conditions like cancer. In this procedure, the provider administers an intra–articular injection of a radioactive substance to destroy the inflamed synovial membrane tissue. Providers may use this procedure to treat chronic hemophilic synovitis, which causes recurrent bleeding in a joint, unresponsive to other treatment.
